#3516. Blizzard Officially Responds to Disappointed Overwatch Fans Over Hero 55

Hero 55 was supposed to bring some Omnic aura to the Support roster; things have changed

Blizzard Entertainment is about to make good on the promise of delivering 10 new heroes to Overwatch in 2026, with the final addition arriving in December. The 10th new hero coming to Overwatch in 2026 is an Omnic detective named Hudson, and he'll arrive alongside the launch of season 6. Hudson was officially revealed on Thursday, but many Overwatch fans aren't pleased with a key aspect of his character.

Originally pitched as a new Support hero for Overwatch, Hudson will instead be part of the hero shooter's Damage (DPS) roster.

Overwatch game director Aaron Keller and associate director Alec Dawson discussed the new hero — the game's 55th overall — during a video interview with creators Emongg and Flats, where the two revealed the character's name and role change. Keller called the role switch a late-in-development "pivot."

"As the hero developed, as we look at the mechanics, how they match with the aesthetic, how they match with who the hero is supposed to be, how they’re supposed to be represented in our game, season 6’s hero will be a DPS," Dawson explained. "He's really fun."

Dawson added, "During development, we iterated a lot, we playtested a lot, and the core mechanic and the thing that we were really falling in love with on this hero didn’t really match with being a support. We kind of leaned into the things we loved the most about the hero, and it definitely fit DPS a lot better. So we’re really excited for him pretty soon."

Overwatch players who wanted a new Support hero were less excited to learn that they weren't getting the cool Omnic detective they were promised. Some called it a "bait and switch." Overwatch currently has 23 damage heroes. Hudson will be the 24th.

On Friday, Keller responded to backlash about Hudson's place on the Overwatch roster, offering more context on the decision to "help players understand it, even as some of them are disappointed."

"When we started work on the detective, he was a Support," Keller said in a thread on X. "But as time went on and the kit continued development we realized that it wasn’t working. Once we tested Hudson as a DPS, the turn around in our feelings for him was instantaneous and dramatic.

"This decision ultimately wasn't whether we release a DPS or a Support hero, it was whether we release a great character or one we didn't believe in. Building Heroes for OW is as much of an art form as a technical challenge. Game dev isn’t always straightforward. Sometimes we need to adapt to create the best version of something. The team is incredibly proud of this Hero. I hope you all feel the same way when he launches in Season 6."

Overwatch season 6 is expected to arrive on Tuesday, Dec. 8.

Blizzard's ambitious plan to release 10 heroes this year may never be repeated, but seasonal releases are sticking

#3514. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3513. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit Was Driven In Part By Cost-Cutting (Report)

It's a bewildering state of affairs over at Warner Bros./DC. After seemingly being welcomed into the newly-formed Skydance (the name of the recently-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount), James Gunn and Peter Safran suddenly stepped down as DC Studios co-heads in a move that came as a shock to pretty much everybody outside of Skydance CEO David Ellison and his colleagues. Now, a report claims the pair's ousting was all part of an attempt to save money, which, considering recent developments, certainly seems plausible.

According to IndieWire, Gunn and Safran's exit was partly "about cost-cutting" as Skydance prepares to tackle its $80 billion debt and deliver the $6 billion in yearly savings over the next three years that Ellison has promised. As the outlet put it, "Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.' film unit," which has struggled to deliver many hits in 2026. We already knew that Skydance had inherited massive flops from the Warner deal (including Tom Cruise's "Digger" and "The Bride!"), but an insider has now told IndieWire that the estimated losses stand at almost $1 billion.

According to the report, this played into Gunn and Safran's dismissal, especially since they oversaw one of the most egregious box office failures of 2026 in "Supergirl." (The Milly Alcock-led movie made just $126.5 million at the box office on a whopping $170 million to $186 million budget.) What's more, sources have informed Page Six that "Supergirl" ultimately lost $135 million. So, while the film's performance was always going to impact whether or not Ellison elected to keep Gunn and Safran in their posts, IndieWire's report has indicated that the cost-saving measures were even more integral to his decision than we previously realized.

After the "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow" debuts in 2027, David Ellison will reportedly dismantle James Gunn's DC Universe, resetting DC's cinematic franchise once again. It's a less than ideal development amid the ongoing superhero fatigue that has already seen the genre fall out of favor with mass audiences. For Ellison, however, it seems the real motivating factor is the same thing as always: money.

What makes Gunn and Peter Safran's exit particularly surprising is that Ellison initially seemed to want to keep them at Skydance. In early October 2026, The Hollywood Reporter cited insiders as claiming the DC Studios co-heads met with Ellison and were asked to stay and "keep doing what you're doing." According to Page Six, however, plans were already in the works to replace the pair with the newly-appointed Jeremy Latcham. One source told the outlet, "It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing."

But as IndieWire points out, not only was Skydance inheriting multiple flops from Warner Bros. generally, Gunn and Safran's deal was "unusually generous." We already knew the pair were reporting directly to ex-Warner CEO David Ellison, who was seemingly content to leave them to it. But these two were also making a tidy profit of their own, with Safran simultaneously heading up his own The Safran Company and Gunn earning big pay days for producing "Supergirl" and "Clayface," and writing and directing both "Superman" and "Man of Tomorrow." According to IndieWire's insiders, Gunn was making as much as $10 million per DC movie.

David Ellison's post-James Gunn and Peter Safran plans make the cost-cutting explanation even more obvious. Jeremy Latcham, who becomes the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1, 2026, will now report to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein instead of directly to Ellison. What's more, one thing we do know about Latcham is that he has a more mainstream sensibility that Gunn's prediction for lesser-known, more off-beat DC properties. What does that mean in Ellison's eyes? A better chance at earning a decent profit when compared with Gunn's plans to give Batman's two most popular Robins their own movie and churn out Mister Miracle animated shows.

Meanwhile, DC Studios hasn't exactly been the biggest money maker under Gunn and Safran. The Man of Steel is one of DC's marquee characters, yet Gunn's "Superman" made $618.7 million in 2025. That's not bad, but for one of DC's most popular characters, it's a little underwhelming (as was the movie). Elsewhere, things have been similarly underwhelming. "Supergirl" was a box office disaster, and the most recent DC release, "Clayface" has done okay, making $111.7 million on a $40 million budget. Bearing in mind this is DC, one of the jewels in the Warner Bros. crown, you can imagine Ellison taking a look at these figures with the weight of his financial commitments and simply deciding to cut Gunn and Safran loose.

For now, Gunn will stick around to oversee the release of 2027's "Man of Tomorrow." According to a source who spoke to Page Six, however, this is only because of Directors Guild of America rules that meant he "could not be removed." If these reports are accurate, Ellison looks to be more intent upon cutting costs than we realized.

How to clean a stainless steel sink and bring back its showroom shine using basic cupboard staples

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you are getting your home ready for festive hosting, do not overlook the sink. Even with pristine worktops and clean floors, cloudy stainless steel covered in chalky water rings instantly makes a kitchen feel tired.

Before the holiday cooking frenzy begins, you can revive a dull basin without scratching the metal or buying pricey specialty cleaners. This five-minute routine cuts through greasy buildup and seals in a bright, showroom shine just in time for visitors.

Rinse away loose food debris, then wash the entire basin thoroughly with hot water and dish soap. Using a soft microfiber cloth or non-scratch sponge, wipe in long, steady strokes that follow the faint brushed grain of the steel rather than scrubbing in circles.

This removes the surface grease film so your cleaning paste can make direct contact with the mineral spots underneath.

Sprinkle a light dusting of baking soda over the damp steel, concentrating on the drain and faucet base where hard water residue gathers. Using a damp cloth, work the powder into a paste along the metal's grain to lift dull water rings without scratching.

For stubborn hard-water marks, rinse the baking soda paste away thoroughly first, then apply a light spray of white vinegar directly to the mineral scale.

Letting the vinegar sit undiluted for a few minutes allows its mild acetic acid to chemically dissolve crusty calcium and magnesium deposits without being neutralized by the alkaline baking soda.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Avoid spraying vinegar onto specialized faucet finishes like matte black, brass, or oil-rubbed bronze, as the acid can strip or discolor the coating.

Once the mineral scale softens, use a soft-bristled brush or non-scratch sponge to gently agitate and lift any remaining gritty buildup from the metal’s surface texture.

Standing water left to evaporate is why cloudy spots return. Use a dry dish towel or microfiber cloth to wipe the entire basin, faucet, and drainboard until completely dry.

For an optional finishing shine, apply a single drop of mineral oil (like baby oil) or olive oil to a soft cloth and buff it into the steel, following the direction of the metal's grain. Buff vigorously with a clean, dry section of the towel until no residue remains.

This creates a light barrier that repels water beads and keeps the shine lasting longer, especially on faucets and handles.

#3511. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3: The Secret Fire Explained

You cannot pass! The dark fire will not avail you, flame of spoilers for "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3, "The Secret Fire."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 does a lot of things right, especially when Sauron is on screen attempting to make a shiny piece of jewelry to master all other pieces of jewelry — all while being haunted by the ghost of Celebrimbor. Indeed, the show shines most when it focuses on the bad guys, like introducing the stunning-looking Nazgnagôl or Adam Young's orc with shifting loyalties and a penchant for poetry.

One thing that is different this season is the lack of mystery identities. We now know very well who Sauron is, we know that The Stranger is actually Gandalf, we finally learn this season who the Dark Wizard is, and we even know why Theo is still in this story. It's as if "The Rings of Power" creators J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay got tired of the waiting around and decided to have god himself come down and explain things directly at the audience.

Well, that is actually exactly what happens in Episode 3, because Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) has an actual burning bush moment and talks to the actual god of J. R. R. Tolkien's Legendarium to learn about the Secret Fire, and his purpose in the story.

In the episode, Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) sends Gandalf on a quest to chase a rabbit. This leads Gandalf to an altar where the rabbit combusts into a flame that speaks to the wizard and explains he is the almighty, whose Secret Fire burns inside every creature on Middle-earth.

Even though "The Rings of Power" is set in a world of magic rings, dragons, dwarves and elves, we have not really seen a lot of thel supernatural — despite it being relatively common in Middle-earth. The world of J. R. R. Tolkien is one of angels and elves that get resurrected, a world that literally goes from flat to round when the creator of all existence gets angry at men and sinks an entire continent to the bottom of the sea.

This is the most overt example of supernatural fantasy we've got in "The Rings of Power" so far, as Gandalf hears a strange voice (Allan Corduner) coming from a manifestation of a flame. The flame gives Gandalf (after calling him by his original Quenya name Olórin) a cosmic vision as the voice reveals itself to be the one who "built the heavens and the stars," that which burns within all living things. As the voice says, "all of Middle-earth is cradled within my flame."

That is the Secret Fire, which is alluded to by Gandalf in the original "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. The Secret Fire, or Flame Imperishable, is Gandalf's higher calling, essentially the power of Tolkien's equivalent of God. Named Erū Ilúvatar, this being is the creator of the whole world, and his Secret Fire is what gives life to the universe. That fire is inside all living beings, and is the thing Morgoth craved most, because he was unable to create life without it, the reason he was driven to the shadow. In Tolkien's world, the Secret Fire is the equivalent of the Holy Spirit in Abrahamic religions, the manifestation of the almighty within all beings.

It is quite funny that "The Rings of Power" has arguably its biggest exposition dump of Season 3 come directly from god, who reveals to Gandalf the entire history of the Istari and reveals the identity of the Dark Wizard. After 2 seasons of audiences trying to work out the identity of the Dark Wizard and his purpose, along drops god from the heavens and just outright explains that he is actually a Blue Wizard and gives audiences the whole backstory in a single scene.

Of course, as shocking as Erū Ilúvatar appearing in "The Rings of Power" is, it makes sense for the show to introduce him now. That's because he has a big role to play in Season 4 and the fall of Númenor. Still, the idea that this show has now officially involved higher beings in the conflict against Sauron is a deep cut concept that separates this from other fantasy shows.

In Tolkien's text, the Valar (essentially the gods of Olympus under Erū Ilúvatar's Zeus) don't get directly involved in the wars of Middle-earth (at least not since Elrond's father convinced the Valar to physically aid in the fight against Morgoth), but their influence and power is felt all throughout the Second Age of Middle-earth and the war against Sauron. "The Rings of Power" leaning more into the supernatural fantasy of Tolkien is one way of making this already quite expansive world even more interesting and complex.

#3510. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

I’m very new to the NCIS franchise, but I think NCIS: New York, which debuted last month on the 2026 television schedule, is really fun. I love the characters and the actors playing them, and that is the most important thing for procedurals to work for me. I especially like Scott Caan’s character, even if it’s really similar to his Hawaii Five-0. There are two subplots that I’m really not digging, but they are easy to wrap up, and I hope the show does that quickly.

My first issue involves two special agents on the team: Addy Ross, played by Jacqueline Byers, and Wyatt Sellers, played by Shane Harper. There is a weird “will they/won’t they” thing going on between the two characters, and I don’t like it. It’s not the chemistry between the actors or the characters or anything like that. It’s just unnecessary. There doesn’t have to be a romantic angle in a show like NCIS: New York. It feels shoehorned in, and doesn’t feel organic at all.

They are the “other” two members of the field team, with Caan and LL Cool J making up the “A-team” as the two biggest stars on the show. Addy and Wyatt are great when they are doing their jobs, and I can even get behind the idea that Wyatt is trying to learn more about the personal life of his partner, who is very private about it. Hinting at a potential relationship is not believable. These are professionals! Keep them professional!

My other big issue with the character subplots is between the two “office” members of the team. Jennifer Beals plays Robyn Wells, the leader of the team, and she’s great! It’s so fun watching her in a new show. However, she has a consistent beef with the computer nerd, Sean Sullivan (Devon Druid). It stems from the reason Druid is employed by NCIS. His backstory hasn’t been fully fleshed out on the show yet, but we do know that he is there because he was a hacker who was facing a long prison sentence.

That’s all well and good, but every time Sean says almost anything about the job, Robyn reminds him that he has prison hanging over her head. Like, I get it. He’s there against his will and avoiding jail. Great! Fun concept! But do we really need to be constantly reminded of it? Let it just sit in the background and come up when it makes sense. The character’s backstory doesn’t need to be re-established all the time.

As I said, both of these stories can be wrapped up, or at least pushed way to the back burner without really causing any plot holes or other problems with the show, and I really hope they are soon. Otherwise, I’m looking forward to NCIS: New York's future

#3507. Marvel Officially Confirms Whether RDJ's Doctor Doom Is A Tony Stark Variant

When Marvel Studios announced Robert Downey Jr. would play Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" fans used one word to describe it: desperate. But anticipation for RDJ's return has only grown as "Doomsday" has drawn nearer. Still, significant confusion remains. After all, Downey Jr.'s best-known role is that of Tony Stark/Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Now, he's back in that same franchise as a supervillain? It's all a bit confounding, really, and while Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige has just tried to clear it all up, he's also somehow made things even more confusing.

Speaking to Empire, Feige was asked whether RDJ is playing a Tony Stark variant in "Doomsday" or an entirely different character. The Marvel Studios boss seemed to indicate the latter is true. "Is Steve Rogers a Johnny Storm variant?" he said in reference to Chris Evans having played both characters at different points throughout Marvel's cinematic history. "People wondered, 'Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?' The answer is no. He's Victor Von Doom."

Evans played Johnny Storm in a an entirely different cinematic universe, specifically portraying the Fantastic Four member in the 20th Century Fox Marvel movies. He then played Steve Rogers/Captain America in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Downey Jr., however, played Tony Stark in the MCU and is now back as Victor Von Doom in that same universe. Sure, the multiverse has made all of this more nebulous. We saw Evans' Johnny Storm in "Deadpool & Wolverine," which means both he and Evans' Steve Rogers could, conceivably, appear together in the MCU. But it would surely feel like a letdown to bring back the most popular and important actor in MCU history as a villain and let that be that.

Doctor Doom was once Iron Man in the comics, and in 2010's "What If? Iron Man: Demon in an Armor" an amnesiac Tony Stark became the supervillain. But Kevin Feige has seemingly confirmed the Victor Von Doom of "Avengers: Doomsday" is like neither of these examples.

According to the Marvel Studios head, Robert Downey Jr. is playing an entirely separate character to Tony Stark, likely thanks to the multiversal incursions that threaten to collapse the universe in "Doomsday." What we'll essentially see, then, is a character named Victor Von Doom who hails from an entirely different timeline to the main MCU (likely the one that gave us 2025's "Fantastic Four: First Steps"), has no connection to Tony Stark, and just happens to look like the former Iron Man. I feel confident in saying that this only raises more questions. Is there another Tony Stark in Doom's timeline? Is there really no connection at all between RDJ's villain and the Iron Man of the MCU?

Regardless, "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo promised Empire that this Doctor Doom will be a truly scary villain, with Joe saying he's "a Gothic character" and "a very powerful character with some very dark magic" who's "not above selling his soul to get what he wants. He's worth being scared of." Interestingly, the co-director added that RDJ's Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he has "lost a child." The only parallel there between Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark and his Doom is that the former was once particularly shaken by losing Tom Holland's Spider-Man to Thanos' snap in 'Avengers: Infinity War." Otherwise, he's never lost a child, which is further proof that this is a different character and not a Tony Stark variant.

According to Joe Russo, those who've seen early screenings of "Avengers: Doomsday" have said "it's a very scary movie" due to Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom being "so profoundly damaged." Clearly, the loss of his child is what drives this particular incarnation of Doom — which puts some of the "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer footage in context. In the trailer, we hear Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman saying, "Victor [...] used to be different. He used to be kind, he used to be caring. And then, everything he loved was taken from him." This is obviously in reference to the loss of his child. In that same trailer, Doom accuses all the heroes of having lived "stolen lives," suggesting that something they did in previous MCU installments might have triggered the event that led to his child's death.

Unfortunately, while Downey Jr. did talk to Empire, he didn't shed much light on the Tony Stark variant question. Instead he talked about Michael Douglas at the end of "Falling Down," saying "He goes, 'I'm the bad guy?' I had that realization a couple of days into shooting 'Doomsday,' because all the heroes are over there, and I'm the problem." The actor recalled having "leaned in" to being the villain and having a "glorious time." That's lovely Rob, but are you Iron Man or not? Otherwise, he described Doom as being on a "scorched earth" mission, adding "Whatever you think he may be entertaining, I would ten times it, and you'll probably be closer to the ballpark."

Did Marvel really bring back RDJ without intending to at least hint at Tony Stark's possible return? It seems unbelievable. For now, we'll have to wait until "Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026 to find out.

#3506. Fallout 5 and Fallout Remasters Officially Announced

Xbox wants more Fallout, and after a yearslong drought of new games, Bethesda Softworks is making it happen. Bethesda plans to release remasters of both Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas for modern platforms, the company said in July in a massive roadmap of the developer's future. Those remasters are part of a larger plan to reinvest in Fallout games — including Fallout 5, which is currently in pre-production — and a new untitled project at Obsidian Entertainment.

"We have multiple Fallout projects in active development right now," Bethesda said in an official announcement this summer. That includes Fallout 5, which is described as the studio's "long-range destination," and "a major Fallout 76 expansion" planned for 2027 called Raven Rock, which will serve as a prequel story to Fallout 3.

Bethesda also confirmed two long-standing rumors, announcing remasters for Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas. The studio did not provide any further details or a release window, but the projects have reportedly been in the works for many years. The existence of a Fallout 3 remaster dates back to at least 2020, when the project's existence was revealed through court documents related to the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) litigation regarding Microsoft's buyout of Activision Blizzard.

Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas' remasters follow last year's release of The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion Remastered, which was co-developed by Virtuos and Bethesda Game Studios. Bethesda also marked the 10-year anniversary of Fallout 4 in 2025, with the release of Fallout 4: Anniversary Edition. That rerelease included the original game, all six of the previously released DLC add-ons, as well as over 150 items pulled from the Fallout 4 Creation Club.

Fallout 3 was originally released in 2008 for PlayStation 3, Windows PC, and Xbox 360. The game was the third major installment in the Fallout series, and the first to be developed by Bethesda after acquiring the rights to the franchise from Interplay Entertainment. Fallout 3 is set in and around Washington D.C. 200 years after a devastating nuclear war, and players control a 19-year-old Vault dweller in search of their missing father.

Fallout: New Vegas followed in 2010, and was developed by Obsidian Entertainment. It was set in the Mojave Desert and casts players as a courier who becomes embroiled in a conflict between various factions who are vying for control of the region.

In addition to new Fallout games, a third season of the Fallout TV series is in the works and recently wrapped filming. Bethesda Game Studios is also hard at work on the next game in its fantasy role-playing game series: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is now in development.

#3505. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

The Odyssey, one of the highest-grossing films of the 2026 movie schedule, is a serious movie that blends mythological themes and modern storytelling as it explores the journey of Odysseus as he faces a dangerous voyage through fantastical realms on his way back to his family. And its director, Christopher Nolan, is a revered filmmaker known for paying attention to little details as he brings his signature narrative and visual style to life on the big screen. That doesn’t mean hilarious behind-the-scenes moments and shenanigans don’t still happen during production, and one in particular involves Tom Holland requesting skirt alterations.

The fantasy epic marked Tom Holland’s first time working with the filmmaker, and boy does he have some memorable stories to share from the experience. For example, according to Variety, who was at the November 10 FYC event, the current Spider-Man decided to take matters of his skirt into his own hands with costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, asking her to hem it to help give him some height on screen.

In the 75-minute documentary Behind the Scenes of The Odyssey, chronicling the making of the three-hour blockbuster, Holland revealed that his reasoning for the change didn’t matter because you can’t sneak anything by Christopher Nolan. He said:

I asked Ellen, the costume designer, I said, ‘Could you just make the skirt a little shorter?’ It’ll make me look a little taller.

Estimated to fall somewhere between 5’6” and 5’8”, I can absolutely understand wanting to appear as tall as possible while starring in such a big movie.

I also appreciate that the Peter Parker actor has enough self-awareness to make such a request. Apparently, he even got the request fulfilled when the costume designer had his tailored skirt ready six weeks later. However, Christopher Nolan noticed that something was amiss and had the following question:

Two seconds into taking in the costume, [Christopher Nolan] was like, ‘How come the skirt is shorter?’

Critics heaped praise on The Odyssey, and the box office numbers reflected that audiences couldn’t get enough, so the length of Tom Holland’s skirt clearly had no effect on the ultimate outcome. But personally, I now wish I knew what the actor’s response was when the Inception director asked what happened. Did he cop to his attempt to look taller on screen? Did he try to play it off in some other way? Did the filmmaker find it as hilarious as I do?

Without a camera turned on them both in that moment, we might never know for sure, but I’m not surprised that someone as meticulous as Christopher Nolan noticed almost immediately and called out the change.

There have already been plenty of memorable stories about the shoot, as Matt Damon talked about being “wet” and “cold” during portions of the production while Charlize Theron acted through massive winds that got up to 30 to 40 miles per hour. Now, I hope we get more silly tales like this one from Tom Holland.

With The Odyssey expected to be a major awards contender this year, I feel like that's very possible. So, here's hoping we get to learn more about Tom Holland trying to shorten his skirt for this Christopher Nolan epic.

#3503. Avengers: Doomsday's Official Writing Credits Confirm Two Major Marvel Cameos

As the December 18 release of "Avengers: Doomsday" rapidly approaches, fan speculation is running rampant over just about every aspect of the movie. Is Doctor Doom a Tony Stark variant? Which characters will die? And who will make surprise cameos? Anthony Mackie recently spoiled the return of Paul Bettany's Vision, while there's also been talk that the finalized Writers Guild of America writing credits would tip the appearances of two hugely popular characters. This talk is now fact.

Those credits are now official, and, per the WGA website, Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron will share the coveted "written by" credit (with an "and" instead of an "&," which means they did not write as a team). Meanwhile, quite a few folks received Additional Literary Material credits (which will not be seen on screen). Here's the list: McFeely, Waldron, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, Destin Daniel Cretton, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman.

Yep, the previously uncredited Reynolds and Jackman will join the spandex showdown as Deadpool and Wolverine. Probably. I mean, it'd be funny if the fellas were hired to punch up Kelsey Grammer's dialogue, but, no, this almost certainly means the indestructible duo is back. As for how significant a role they'll play in "Avengers: Doomsday," your guess is as good as mine. So let's get to guessin'!

My greatest fear regarding "Avengers: Doomsday" is that it'll be undone by superhero clutter. If the Russos don't have a compelling story (and we know they began shooting without a finished script), it could be a comic book version of those leaden 1960s all-star romps like "Casino Royale," "Candy" and "The Magic Christian," where each actor's sole function is to pop up on camera so the viewer can say "Hey, there's Orson Welles!"

I've been encouraged by some of what I've heard over the last month – in particular, that James Marsden's Cyclops plays a significant role in the film. If this means we'll get a resumption of hostilities between the humorless Scott Summers and cocky Logan, I'll be so very happy. Add the exponentially more antagonistic Deadpool into the mix, and that just may be enough to drive Summers into the steely arms of Doctor Doom.

I'm most excited to see Deadpool be the straw that stirs the drink. I really don't want a relentlessly dour "Avengers: Doomsday," which is the vibe I'm getting from the pea green aesthetic of the trailers (and its fast food tie-ins). Are they going to get MCU fans to buy back in with a surfeit of character deaths? Gunn's "Superman" caught on because it foregrounded hope in a thoughtful, non-anodyne way. We live in bleak times. I'm not sure AI-friendly filmmakers like the Russos should be in charge of a franchise that, overall, appeals to our sense of humanity. I'm hoping the heavy-handed trailers are a happy bait-and-switch. Let Deadpool and Wolverine cook.

#3501. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3500. Rings Of Power Season 3 Features The Most Gruesome TV Scene Of 2026

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" is a tragedy. As far as prequels go, this one is not as full of doom and gloom as "Andor" — a show where audiences knew the main character was destined to die tragically — but it is still a show all about the rise of an evil that almost conquered Middle-earth. Indeed, though there are some surprising main characters in Season 3, the true star of "Rings of Power" is the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers), who spends each season lying and manipulating his way to ruining everyone else's day.

This was especially prominent than in Season 2, which was all about Sauron making the elves believe he was an envoy of the Valar so that they'd help him make the titular Rings of Power. In particular, Sauron spent the entire season gaslighting the show's best and most tragic character, Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards). Episode after episode, Sauron used Celebrimbor's vanity and pride to his advantage, scheming and lying into making Celebrimbor his friend and ally, before stabbing him in the chest with a pike.

This leads to "Rings of Power" Season 3 featuring the most gruesome TV scene of 2026. When Sauron returns to his little office in Barad-dûr after failing to make the One Ring yet again, the Dark Lord gets a visit from the ghost of Celebrimbor, who mocks Sauron's failures at trying to replicate the dead elven smith's work.

And right there, in front of Sauron, is the rotting body of Celebrimbor, hanging on a wall like a trophy.

What makes this horrifying is not only that Sauron still keeps the dead body of Celebrimbor around, but the fact that it's a rotting mess with arrows sticking out of the torso. Making matters worse, Skelebrimbor is hung from a wall like a war banner

This, of course, is a reference to the actual books. As J.R.R. Tolkien himself wrote, Celebrimbor's dead body was "hung upon a pole, shot through with Orc-arrows" and turned upon Elrond's forces like a banner for Sauron's army. It's why fans affectionately refer to this act as "Celebrimbanner." It is arguably one of the cruelest things the Dark Lord ever did — which is saying something considering the untold number of people that died because of him.

Seeing the body of Celebrimbor hanging on a wall — the flesh rotting away, an expression of fear and shock on the skeleton — is horrifying, and easily the most gruesome piece of imagery in the entire "Lord of the Rings" franchise. There is no reason why Sauron needs to have kept the body of Celebrimbor, other than to assert his cruelty.

And yet, it leads to a rather hilarious scene of the ghost of Celebrimbor appearing only to taunt Sauron, ragebaiting the Dark Lord and mocking his inability to craft anything as majestic as the great smith Celebrimbor. He even tells Sauron that his orcs now pity him because of how pathetic his jewelry crafting skills are. It's a testament to Charlie Vickers for the subtle ways in which you can tell the insults are actually getting at Sauron. Meanwhile Charles Edwards reminds us why he is one of the best pieces of casting in this show, with this short but impactful scene in a third season that otherwise struggles to live up to hype.

#3499. HBO’s 5-Part Crime Drama Has One of the Best Seasons in TV History

The Wire’s fourth season provided a far deeper look at Baltimore’s problems

The Wire’s fourth season provided a far deeper look at Baltimore’s problems

At the turn of the 21st century, HBO was the place for prestige crime drama. The launch of The Sopranos in 1999 paved the way for the 2002 premiere of The Wire, which focused on drug dealers in Baltimore and the police officers trying to disrupt their operations. The series is still one of the best shows of all time, and provided breakout roles for huge stars like Idris Elba and Michael B. Jordan. But while it was compelling from the beginning, The Wire truly achieved perfection in season 4 when the scope expanded beyond the drug trade to examine the cycle of institutional failure.

Season 1 of The Wire was tightly focused on the drug empire of Avon Barksdale (Wood Harris) and his business-savvy second-in-command Stringer Bell (Elba). Showrunner David Simon quickly established a brilliant mix of humor and pathos. The show could find comedy in something as simple as cops struggling to get new furniture into their office, and then gut audiences with the death of a relatable drug dealer. Season 2 shifted the focus to the city’s port system, a jarring change as many characters faded into the background to make room for the tragic tale of the Sobotka family. Season 3 was the most tightly linked to the show’s first season, largely completing the story of the Barksdale gang.

That made season 4 perfect for a soft reboot, a shift that was defined by star Dominic West all but disappearing after his relentless detective, Jimmy McNulty, was demoted for pissing off his bosses too many times. The detectives he previously worked with in the major crimes unit continue their work, investigating a vicious new gang that’s filling the void Barksdale left behind. Lester Freamon (Clarke Peters) effectively steps into the McNulty role of pursuing the truth, even when his supervisors would love for him to be a little less dogged, bringing a new methodical nature to the investigations instead of McNulty’s brash confidence. But while the cops vs. criminals beats are familiar, they become just one part of a far more ambitious season that fully capitalized on Simon’s knowledge of the city. (Simon worked as a journalist at The Baltimore Sun for 12 years before creating The Wire.)

The season’s largest secondary plot involves the students at a Baltimore middle school where former cop Roland Pryzbylewski (Jim True-Frost) begins teaching. The young actors do a phenomenal job establishing likable characters in terrible circumstances. You want to root for all of them, from the ambitious Randy Wagstaff (Maestro Harrell) to the fiercely protective Michael Lee (Tristan Wilds). By the end of season 4, the system has profoundly failed almost all of these kids, driving them to lives of addiction and violence. The Wire was always good at making most of its characters sympathetic, but seeing children trapped in such a brutal cycle really drives home the show’s themes of how crime thrives when institutions fail.

That theme also plays out in the mayoral campaign of Tommy Carcetti (Aidan Gillen). Carcetti was introduced in season 3 as an ambitious city council member, but he really shines in season 4 as he runs on reforming the Baltimore Police Department — and then quickly breaks his promises. Gillen’s oily performance as a political survivor who would doom his city to satisfy his own ambitions was what landed him the role of Littlefinger in Game of Thrones. Carcetti is even more compelling a character because he feels like a man who could have done good if he’d been willing to make sacrifices rather than feed his own ego.

The Wire season 4 is able to build so many new arcs because of the strong foundation established in the previous three seasons. The show is dense with rich characters who have grown significantly over the years even as they continue to struggle with many of the same problems. The cops and drug dealers alike feel world-weary as they deal with a more violent new generation represented by Marlo Stanfield (Jamie Hector) and his vicious enforcers Snoop (Felicia Pearson) and Chris Partlow (Gbenga Akinnagbe). Combined with the dark fate of most of the kids and Carcetti’s broken promises, the season creates the bleak feeling that everyone is trapped in a cycle of misery and decay.

Season 5 gave most of The Wire’s characters satisfying ends to their arcs and delivered a scathing critique of the downfall of American newspapers, commentary that has only become more profound 20 years later. But overall, it’s a big step down from season 4, spending too much time on a goofy fake serial killer plot and not enough on the nuanced character-driven stories that made season 4 feel so authentic. There are no bad seasons of The Wire, but season 4 perfectly achieved the show’s goals. It’s an alternately funny, tragic, and profound look at the complex ways that people are betrayed by systems that never really give them a chance to succeed.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

My wife and I wrapped up season 3 of the Wire two days before I began my career as a NYC teacher. We held off on season 4 until I was sure I could survive. My work has been plenty bleak at times but never this bleak. Although there was an article in the Times a week before the COVID shutdown that explicated how vital the NYC DOE was as a social safety net, and that made me feel both great and depressed.

Netflix put out a ton of content in 2026, and it's not showing any signs of slowing down. Case in point: those with a Netflix subscription can watch Jessica Chastain's new thriller movie Heartland this weekend. The movie is set in Nashville, and filmed some scenes right in the heart of Broadway. Director Shana Feste spoke to CinemaBlend about this experience, and one problem they kept having during production in the country music destination.

In Heartland Jessica Chastain was deep into character playing Misty Jones, a washed up (Grammy-winning) country singer. After living in seclusion for years she returns to Nashville in search of her missing niece Charlie Heart, played by real-life country singer Carter Faith. As you can see in the video above, I spoke to director Shana Feste about shooting on location, where she told me:

We were a big movie, but we weren't that big. So it's not like we could really shut anything down. So we just went on to Lower Broadway right in the middle of like chaos. And we got our truck and we just, I think we didn't even have really any camera equipment. So we used the like, what is that? The lever from the, one of the big trucks, whatever it's called. We just put our camera on that and we like pressed down and he like went, so we had this big top shot and then it like went into the audience.

Nashville is a big vacation destination, and most of the action happens on Broadway. As such, there are ton of people there at any given day, going to the various bars, restaurants, and music venues throughout the strip. Feste wanted to make sure Heartland captured that energy, which is why there were a number of scenes shot in Nashville itself. Although it was a bit of a logistical challenge.

Chastain crushed it in the movie's 114-minute runtime, with the Oscar-winner transforming her body and voice into Misty. Still, filming in Nashville had challenges, including one common issue with the background actors. As Feste went on to say:

I mean, the hardest thing was getting people to like stop looking at the camera and just like walk naturally because you're, it's like shooting a Las Vegas strip, you know? It's like pure chaos. But that is what I wanted to include in the movie.

Between the busy street traffic and folks looking directly into camera, those days in Nashville were not without roadblocks. Although having seen Heartland before it arrived on Netflix this weekend, I think it was totally worth it. The energy was electric, and helped to make the new streaming film all the more immersive.

When speaking with Feste about shooting on location, there was one other factor that I couldn't stop thinking about. Namely all the Bachelorette Parties that are happening in Nashville on any given day. The Run Sweetheart Run director confirmed they were part of the equation, offering:

Oh total bachelorette parties. So funny that you say that. A lot of the actual background players that we got to choose like and dress that we threw into the world were... I had like six bachelorette parties. So we provided all those costumes.

It sounds like shooting in Nashville isn't for the faint of heart, but the cast and crew of Heartland were ultimately able to pull it off. It helps give the new movie a tactile and real time and place, especially as Misty searches the town in search of her niece Charlie.

Folks can see it all for themselves, as Heartland is on Netflix as part of the 2026 movie release list. Jessica Chastain crushes her role as the film's protagonist, including belting out a few country musical numbers. After all, this is Nashville we're talking about.

#3497. I tested the DJI Osmo 360 II and Insta360 needs to be seriously scared

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The DJI Osmo 360 II is the first (and, as I write this, the only) 360 camera to shoot 8K at 60fps. This makes it my top choice for high-octane 360 footage like motovlogging or extreme sports. Unlike its predecessor, the 360 II has user-replaceable lenses, and while battery life isn’t mind-blowing, it’s good enough at 8K/60fps. The only things I don’t like about the Osmo 360 II are its sky-high U.S. price and the internal audio wind reduction, which isn’t anything to write home about.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

“Uh oh,” is what Insta360 will doubtless have thought when the DJI Osmo 360 II launched. And it should’ve been worried. Up to now, Insta360 has been the undisputed king of 360 tech. But that reign has come to an end.

It all comes down to one thing: 8K/60fps, which the DJI Osmo 360 II can shoot. The flagship Insta360 X6, meanwhile, cannot, topping out at 8K/50fps. Insta360 is simply not there yet with the tech, and in fairness, that’s understandable. 8K at 60fps in 360 degrees puts extreme demands on a pocket-sized camera, its processor, memory, battery and thermals.

But somehow DJI has achieved it – which means it’s now ahead in the race. Even if the Osmo 360 II isn’t the best 360 camera in every area, it does the most important thing right now. It gives content creators the flexibility of 4K reframing from 360 footage at a frame rate fast enough for high-octane footage, and usable enough for YouTube.

So should you buy this camera? Find out in my full DJI Osmo 360 II review.

Unsurprisingly, given this is a flagship 360 camera, the Osmo 360 II isn’t cheap, opening the register at a whopping $699 in the U.S. at Amazon for the standard bundle with basic accessories. If you want accessories, the Adventure Combo I tested, with extra batteries and a selfie stick, costs $829. Of course, this is thanks to U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. It’s also worth noting that, resulting from its feud with the U.S. government, DJI has withdrawn first-party support in the States, meaning no care plans if the camera needs repair.

In the U.K., the Osmo 360 II starts at £509, which undercuts the Insta360 X6 by over £100. And U.K. consumers also get access to a wider range of accessories bundles at Amazon, so they can tailor their spend to exactly what they need.

This pricing is comparable to the Insta360 X6, which also starts at $699. In my opinion, the 360 II is a much better buy thanks to the higher 60fps frame rate. In the U.K., where the 360 II is both more powerful and cheaper, it’s a total no-brainer. If you’re on a tighter budget, though, I’d advise checking out the Insta360 X5 ($549), GoPro MAX2 ($499) or the OG DJI Osmo 360 ($494). All shoot 8K 360 footage, just not at 60fps.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Osmo 360 II is designed more or less the same as its predecessor. It looks the same, measures the same, and weighs the same. That means it’s a squat-looking thing, especially compared to the lankier X6. It isn’t small though, at 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches, nor is it light at 6.4 ounces, so if you’re after something more suited to mounting on a helmet, check out an action camera like the DJI Osmo Action 6.

Versus the OG Osmo 360, there have been no radical updates to the display, which still isn’t an OLED; no updates to the internal memory, which is still 105GB (although over double the X6’s 47GB); and no updates to waterproofing, which is rated at 33 feet (half the 66 feet of the X6).

The controls are essentially the same, with two buttons on the back for recording and mode changing, a power button, and most tweaks done via the menu system or app. I found the Osmo 360 II’s record button fiddly to press with gloves on. And while I like DJI’s menu, it’s a little busy-feeling on the small display — the X6’s bigger display makes it slightly easier to use in the heat of the moment. Overall though, no major complaints controls-wise.

The Osmo 360 II uses the same quick-release mounting system as the previous gen, plus other DJI cameras like the Osmo Action 5 Pro, Action 6 and Osmo Nano. However, DJI has made a welcome quality-of-life update: the mount is now bi-directional. Previously, you had to get the mount the correct way round, which was annoying, but now it doesn’t matter. It may not sound like a big deal, but it’s kinda like going from USB-A to USB-C and makes the camera a lot quicker and easier to mount-unmount during shooting.

Again, the Osmo 360 II has no major updates to connectivity, with wireless data transfer, USB-C transfer and charging, and 105GB of internal memory, which should get you around 90 minutes of 8K footage — fantastic when you fill or forget a card. There’s Bluetooth and 2.4G for pairing to your phone, but DJI has added NFC connectivity which means you can pair the Osmo 360 II to your phone instantly just by placing the two together.

Where there has been a substantive update is lenses. The original Osmo 360 had non-replaceable lenses, which was a major drawback given all the competition had replaceable ones. 360 lenses are very easy to damage (in fact, my OG 360 was hit by a rock from a semi truck during testing, and DJI had to supply me with a replacement), so replaceable lenses are a huge deal.

The Osmo 360 had to be sent back to DJI for repair, which would be fine if you purchased a DJI care plan… only, you couldn’t buy one of those in the U.S. due to DJI’s ongoing feud with the federal government.

Thankfully, the simple solution has been employed, and the Osmo 360 II has replaceable lenses. Annoyingly, you can’t find official DJI replacement kits on Amazon (another repercussion of that feud with the government). In the U.K., this isn’t an issue, and an official DJI lens replacement kit will cost you just £22 at Amazon.

As always these days, DJI’s stabilization is pretty darn good. In most reframed 360 footage, you’ll be cropping a full 360 view down quite a bit, giving ample headroom for software stabilization (which is applied automatically by the app/desktop app in post production). I noticed a few jitters in wider fields of view, but nothing major.

In single-lens mode, the camera uses DJI’s usual RockSteady in-camera stabilization, and it works a treat. As you can see in the single-lens footage below, everything is beautifully smooth.

The Osmo 360 II’s headline feature is the most important: 8K/60fps. When recording high-octane footage, which is what 360 cameras are commonly used for, 60fps is a fast enough frame rate for smooth-looking footage. Fast-paced footage looks great at 60fps, with no choppiness whatsoever.

The original Osmo 360 and Insta360 X6 could only shoot at up to 50fps, which they might as well not do. 50fps is better than 30fps at smoothing out fast-moving footage, but is only really applicable to European television operating at 50Hz. The standards for online content, like YouTube, are 60fps for high octane and 30fps for everything else.

Thanks to 8K 360 footage, there’s also enough resolution headroom to reframe to 16:9 and maintain 4K when exporting. This all means that the Osmo 360 II is the first (and, as I write, only) 360 camera to let you shoot high-octane footage at high resolution and at a high frame rate.

The dual sensors in the 360 II are the same 1/1.1-Inch Square CMOS sensors as the OG 360. Frame rate is mainly decided by a camera’s image processing capabilities, and so that’s where the improvements have been made.

Unsurprisingly, given DJI is no newcomer to all this, footage looks excellent. The lenses are sharp, while colors look vivid but natural — more natural than Insta360’s typically saturated look.

Obviously, as a 360 camera, the primary benefit is ultimate framing flexibility. Shoot first, choose your fields of view and camera angles later. Aside from the selfie stick dead spot under the camera (which always shows on 360 cameras), stitching wasn’t noticeable, even at ultra-wide FoVs or in 360 modes like ‘Tiny Planet’, which is great.

With the new processing comes 14.5 stops of dynamic range. As such, the Osmo 360 II handles radical shifts in lighting very well, maintaining shadow detail and decreasing the frequency of blown-out highlights. This also benefits low-light performance, with the Osmo 360 II proving a substantial step up over its predecessor. in the equivalent SuperNight mode on both cameras at 8K/30p, the Osmo 360 II's footage looks brighter, sharper and less noisy than the OG Osmo 360. A solid upgrade, helped by the new processors.

Like most 360 cameras, you can also shoot in single-lens mode at up to 4K/120fps, using the Osmo 360 II like a traditional action cam. There’s a new mode called ‘Boost’ video which supposedly offers better quality than the normal video mode.

I asked DJI about this, but it was fairly tight-lipped on the technical explanation, telling me the mode simply widens the field of view to use more of the sensor — presumably the camera then oversamples the 4K output for a sharper image. As the whole (or most of) the sensor is being used, stabilization is affected, so standard video mode is better for shakier scenarios.

The Osmo 360 II packs some useful features for professional users or hardcore creators, including 10-bit color for extra flexibility when editing, and D-Log M for wider dynamic range capture when footage is going to be graded in post later.

The Osmo 360 II introduces a wind-shielded mic, helping to physically reduce wind buffeting alongside the in-camera wind reduction software algorithms. Overall, wind reduction is fine. There are three modes: ‘Standard’, ‘High’ and ‘Smart’ (which automatically adjusts between the first two). If you’re shooting in particularly windy conditions, like motorcycling, ‘High’ works well to reduce wind noise, although the microphones didn’t handle the loud noise of an engine particularly well, with some clipping — you can dial in some minus gain to help with this.

I wouldn’t say the Osmo 360 II’s internal audio is much better or worse than the X6, although both lose out to the Insta360 X5 — despite being a generation old now, the X5 still packs the best internal audio of any 360 camera I’ve tested.

Naturally, as a DJI product, the Osmo 360 II can hook up wirelessly over OsmoAudio to wireless DJI mics, like the DJI Mic 3 or DJI Mic Mini 2S. As they share an ecosystem, you get lots of control over the mics in-camera — control you wouldn’t get by simply connecting over Bluetooth. OsmoAudio is essentially Bluetooth, so audio quality in high dynamic range environments (like motorcycling) isn’t fantastic, but is more than enough for quieter scenarios and vlogging.

The DJI Mimo smartphone app is fairly solid these days. A few years back it was rather basic, but DJI has made strides to compete with Insta360’s app and the GoPro Quik app. There’s not much between them now, although Insta360’s app remains the easiest and most intuitive to use, especially for a straight-to-social workflow.

Mimo gives you a wide range of editing features, effects and export settings. It lets you do the basics, but I find reframing via keyframes a lot more clunky on Mimo versus the Insta360 app. Mimo feels more like a tool for whipping together quick client previews, assuming you’ll finesse footage later on a desktop. The Insta360 app makes it easier to put out smooth, polished content directly from your phone.

DJI has a big advantage for pros and serious creators, though. Both Insta360 and DJI offer desktop editing apps for more serious editing. However, pros will need their camera to fit in with existing workflows, and while both brands offer Premiere Pro 360 plug-ins, only DJI has them for DaVinci Resolve.

The Osmo 360 II’s battery life is a mixed bag. It features a bigger battery than the original Osmo 360, boosted from 1,950mAh to 2,150mAh. Despite this, in my standardized indoor tests, the Osmo 360 II only managed 88 minutes at 8K/30fps versus 112 minutes on the original model. Both pale in comparison to the 2,600mAh Insta360 X6, which managed 117 minutes at 8K/30fps.

That said, the OG model dropped off a cliff at higher frame rates. At 8K/50fps, the original camera only managed 30 minutes in my testing. The Osmo 360 II ran for 66 minutes at 8K/60fps and while it overheated after 45 minutes, it disabled its screen and ran for a further 21 minutes until dying. You’ll get longer while on the move, as wind chill will mean less thermal throttling. Still, 8K/60fps is no easy task, so 66 minutes is impressive.

At 8K/50fps, the Osmo 360 managed 77 minutes and overheated after around 50 (but again soldiered on, thermally throttled, for another 25 minutes. The X6 managed 90 minutes at 8K/50fps, but overheated every 20 minutes.

At 4K/60fps in single-lens mode, the Osmo 360 managed just over 80 minutes. Again, in the indoor stress test conditions, it overheated and thermally throttled itself after around 50 minutes, but kept on shooting for another half an hour before dying. Windchill will solve this. The X6, meanwhile, overheated at 33 minutes and only managed 56 minutes in total at 4K/60fps. Like I said, the Osmo 360 II’s battery life is a mixed bag, but where it counts at 60fps, it’s impressive.

Oof. When I reviewed the original Osmo 360, my sentiment was: “It’s a good start, but needs work.” Well, DJI has done the work, and a lot of it. The Osmo 360 II is the first 360 camera to reach 8K/60fps, making it ideal for creators who want the benefits of 360 recording without sacrificing frame rate.

The Osmo 360 II isn’t perfect, and whether you need this or the Insta360 X6 will, to a large extent, depend on what you’re doing or shooting. If your priority is a straight-to-social workflow, Insta360 still has the edge.

However, the margins between the two are mostly minor, all except one: frame rate. If you shoot high-octane footage — motovlogging, snowboarding, skydiving, etc. — there’s now only one camera to recommend. It has to be the Osmo 360 II.

When he's not snapping away on his beloved Fujifilm camera, he can usually be found telling everyone about his greyhounds, riding his motorcycle, squeezing as many FPS as possible out of PC games, and perfecting his espresso shots.

#3496. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.
