#3495. 5 Best TV Shows Like The Good Daughter

This article contains discussions of addiction, domestic violence, mental health, and sexual assault.

There's a new dark crime thriller on Peacock, and if you haven't watched "The Good Daughter" yet, prepare yourself — this show is unrelentingly distressing, but it'll keep you captivated from beginning to end.

Two of film and television's most talented actresses, Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne, lead this series — based on a book by thriller writer Karin Slaughter, who also created the show — about sisters Charlotte and Samantha Quinn, respectively. As teenagers, Charlotte and Samantha endure a horrifying tragedy when their mother is shot and killed in front of them in their home by masked intruders, after which both girls are also attacked. Years later, Charlotte is working in their hometown of Pikeville, Georgia, with their father Rusty (Brendan Gleeson), a defense attorney whose work may or may not have caused the home invasion that killed his wife and the mother of his children, and Sam lives in New York City as a patent attorney who's trying to escape her past. When a new tragedy strikes in Pikeville and Charlotte gets a front-row seat to the carnage, the sisters reunite under difficult circumstances, unpack their family trauma, and ultimately work together to prove that a teenage girl is innocent.

If you finish binge-watching "The Good Daughter" and want to keep the crime drama streak going, I've got some follow-up suggestions for you. You may notice that "Pieces of Her" and "Will Trent," two other high-profile Slaughter adaptations, don't appear here; the former just barely missed the cut in favor of some other picks, and the latter is very tonally different (largely because it's a network drama). Check your trigger warnings and then try out these five shows you'll like if you loved "The Good Daughter."

Gillian Flynn's most famous novel might be "Gone Girl," which got an incredible film adaptation, but don't sleep on her debut novel and its small-screen adaptation. "Sharp Objects," which dropped on HBO in 2018 and was helmed by the late, great Jean-Marc Vallée and "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" alum Marti Noxon.

After a girl goes missing in her hometown of Wind Gap, Missouri, in the aftermath of a different young woman's murder, journalist Camille Preaker (Amy Adams) — who struggles with serious trauma, her mental health, compulsive self-harm, and an alcohol addiction — reluctantly goes back to Wind Gap and reunites with her controlling Southern belle mother Adora Crellin (an imperious, perfect Patricia Clarkson). When the missing girl's body is discovered shortly thereafter, Camille attempts to solve the murder, tangling with big city detective Richard Willis (Chris Messina, reuniting with Adams after their much less intense film "Julie & Julia") as well as her impulsive and rebellious younger half-sister Amma Crellin (Eliza Scanlon).

Vallée and Noxon create an airless, claustrophobic environment in Wind Gap as Camille tries to face her demons head-on and figure out who's responsible for the deaths of multiple girls ... whose bodies are often missing teeth when they're found. With an ending that'll leave your jaw on the floor and a performance from Adams that should have, by all rights, handed her an Emmy — to say nothing of the magnificent turn from Clarkson — "Sharp Objects" is a must-watch no matter what. Its themes of family trauma pair perfectly with "The Good Daughter."

Philadelphia local Brad Inglesby, who's also the mind behind "Task," created and wrote "Mare of Easttown," which is set in a fictional suburb of Philly called Easttown and hit HBO in 2021. (Confusingly, there is a Philadelphia suburb called Easttown, but it's not the one depicted in the show. Try to keep up!) Kate Winslet stacks accent upon accent as the titular Marianne "Mare" Sheehan, a local detective tasked with investigating the murder of a young single mother, as she continues to try and track down a different missing girl whose case has gone mostly cold. On top of all of that, Mare tragically lost her son years prior, and she lives with her own guilt and grief every day as she also tries to deal with her surviving family, especially her difficult mother, Helen Fahey (Jean Smart), and provides support for her best friend, Lori Ross (Julianne Nicholson).

As Mare teams up with county detective Colin Zabel (a phenomenal Evan Peters, who really nails this tricky accent), struggles to parent her rebellious daughter Siobhán (Angourie Rice) with her ex-husband Frank (David Denman), and tries to solve the murder of said single mother Erin McMenamin (Cailee Spaeny), she also has to deal with her own trauma. Like in "The Good Daughter," Mare's past frequently gets in her way as she attempts to deal with her present, and like "The Good Daughter," the ending of "Mare of Easttown" is as satisfying as it is devastating and sobering. Speaking of "Task," by the way, the shows are set in the same universe ... and Nicholson actually reprised her role as Lori on Inglesby's other series in 2026.

Liane Moriarty has been writing exceptionally sharp and deceptively dark thriller novels for decades now, but thanks to a high-profile adaptation of her 2014 novel "Big Little Lies" in 2017, that book is arguably her most popular by a mile. Jean-Marc Vallée also worked on this series (which was created by David E. Kelley), which moves the novel's story from a ritzy neighborhood in Australia to an exclusive and wealthy community in Monterey, California, populated by mothers like Madeline Mackenzie (Reese Witherspoon), Celeste Wright (Nicole Kidman), and Renata Klein (Laura Dern). When newcomer Jane Chapman (Shailene Woodley) moves to town with her precocious son Ziggy (Iain Armitage), Madeline and Celeste welcome her into the fold with open arms, and as the women bond, it's revealed that they're all struggling in various ways.

Madeline is remarried to Ed (Adam Scott) but shares a daughter, Abigail (Kathryn Newton), with her ex-husband Nathan (James Tupper) ... whose new wife, Bonnie (Zoë Kravitz), irks Madeline to no end. Renata's daughter has been hurt by someone at school, and she blames Ziggy, but the culprit remains at large. Celeste's handsome husband Perry (Alexander Skarsgård) seems perfect, but he's physically abusive behind closed doors; as for Jane, she suffered a devastating sexual assault that resulted in Ziggy but still haunts her years later. As the women's stories converge in entirely unexpected ways, all their problems hit a crisis point ... but they stick together under duress. Yes, the second season of "Big Little Lies" was terrible, and I'm extremely apprehensive about the third season that's in the works — but as far as that first season that was intended as a miniseries, it's unimpeachable and completely complementary to "The Good Daughter."

Another deliciously dark drama that's exclusively available on Peacock, "All Her Fault," adapted from a novel by Andrea Mara, opens as working mother Marissa Irvine ("Succession" veteran and Emmy winner Sarah Snook) goes to pick her young son Milo (Duke McCloud) up from a playdate with a new friend at school. When she gets to the house, she's met by an older woman who's never heard of Marissa or Milo, and before long, Marissa discovers that Milo is missing. After frantically calling her husband Peter (Jake Lacy), the search for Milo begins, and even with her best friend and business partner Colin Dobbs (Jay Ellis) and Peter's troubled but well-meaning sister Lia (Abby Elliott) by her side, Marissa feels adrift and understandably terrified. That's when she turns to her fellow working mother Jenny Kaminsky (Dakota Fanning), who not only understands what Marissa goes through every day as a woman attempting to juggle work and motherhood, but is an invaluable source of support during the most frightening time of Marissa's life.

It's a credit to the bones of Mara's story that, even in its most heightened moments, "All Her Fault" manages to avoid melodrama or absurdity; in fact, it's really grounded by Snook's emotional but intense performance, and Lacy, Fanning, Elliott, Ellis, and supporting players Michael Peña and Sophia Lillis also turn in absolutely incredible performances as a detective and Jenny's nanny, respectively. "All Her Fault" shares a lot more with "The Good Daughter" than a streaming platform — long-held family secrets play enormous roles in both shows — and it's a perfect follow-up.

"The Better Sister," which has a home on Amazon Prime Video, is adapted from a novel by Alafair Burke and premiered in 2025 with showrunner Olivia Milch at the helm. The premise is simple but deeply unsettling: Magazine editor Chloe Taylor (Jessica Biel) is happily married to Adam Macintosh (Corey Stoll), but when he's murdered, she's forced to reunite with her troubled sister and Adam's ex-wife Nicky Macintosh (Elizabeth Banks) as the two try to figure out what happened.

The two lead stars are pretty perfect together as two polar-opposite sisters. As Nicky struggles with an alcohol addiction and tries to get her life together, Chloe's quest for perfection drives a wedge between them. Banks and Biel are joined by performers like Kim Dickens, Matthew Modine, Gloria Reuben, Lorraine Toussaint, and Janel Moloney. Their names are sort of similar, but ultimately, both "The Good Daughter" and "The Better Sister" center on sisterhood ... and all its ups and downs.

#3494. Stacy Keach Played A Villain In One Of The Best Batman Movies Of All Time

Actor Stacy Keach passed away on November 10, 2026, leaving behind a huge list of film, television, and theatre credits across his lifetime. Typecasting never really caught up with Keach. He could play diametrically different characters, like how he acted as both the morally upright Warden Henry Pope in "Prison Break" and Neo-Nazi leader Cameron Alexander in "American History X."

Even so, Keach's deep voice often coded him as a tough guy you don't want to mess with. DC Comics and Batman fans will recognize that voice from "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm," one of the best Batman movies, animated or otherwise. The titular villain is a skull-masked, scythe-wielding vigilante targeting gangsters in Gotham City. Unlike Batman (Kevin Conroy), the Phantasm employs lethal force.

Keach voices the Phantasm (at least when they're wearing their mask). The Phantasm doesn't say that much, admittedly, because silence serves their menacing presence more. But whenever the Phantasm first appears in a plume of smoke, they announce themselves with this line: "[Name], your angel of death awaits!" Keach makes the Phantasm's voice live up to those words. It's deep and ghostly, with an echo that sounds like he is genuinely an apparition from beyond the mortal plane.

"Mask of the Phantasm" features a dual timeline structure; half of the movie takes place in Bruce Wayne's youth before he becomes Batman. He romances Andrea Beaumont (Dana Delany), the woman he almost chose over becoming Batman. Keach has a second role in this storyline as Carl Beaumont, Andrea's financier father. Naturally, you then make the leap (subconsciously or not) in thinking that Carl is the Phantasm, especially once we learn he was once indebted to the gangsters the Phantasm is killing in the present. That's just what the movie wants you to think.

Okay, enough hiding behind spoilers: The Phantasm is actually Andrea herself. She and her father had to flee the country to dodge his loan shark debtors, which is why she canceled her engagement to Bruce all those years ago. But the gangsters caught up to the Beaumonts, killed Carl, and now Andrea is back for revenge. (Amusingly, the twist of Andrea being the Phantasm was spoiled by some tie-in toys.)

Keach's part as Carl gets back to his acting range. He plays, essentially, the Grim Reaper and a terrified father, and he's great in both parts. The red herring of Carl being the Phantasm becomes text late in the movie, after Andrea and Bruce rekindle their relationship and she explains why she left him — except for the part that her dad is dead. Diegetically, Andrea has given her alter ego her father's voice to throw suspicion off herself. While framing her father might dishonor his memory, she's also playing the part of Carl Beaumont's vengeful spirit to kill his killers.

Batman having a romantic connection with a foe is nothing new — just ask Catwoman or Talia al Ghul. The Phantasm's backstory has the foundation for a redemption, but happy endings are hard to come by in Gotham City. "Mask of the Phantasm" commits to being a romantic tragedy; Batman doesn't reach or redeem Andrea, who chooses her vengeance. The final two scenes of the film show Andrea and then Bruce, both alone again. But at least Batman still has Gotham.

"Mask of the Phantasm" remains widely beloved and is often considered the late Kevin Conroy's greatest performance as Batman. Stacy Keach as the Phantasm was an essential ingredient, too, and may he also rest in peace.

When it comes to the 9-1-1 Universe, you never know what to expect, especially with all of the crazy emergencies that are involved. As the franchise continues on the 2026 TV schedule with Season 10 of the Mothership and Season 2 of 9-1-1: Nashville, the stakes are getting higher. What’s also getting higher is the chances of crossovers. Already this season, there was a mini crossover between the two shows, and now it seems like another 9-1-1 crossover is coming, and it involves Ryan Phillippe and Jennifer Love Hewitt.

Phillippe joined 9-1-1: Nashville for Season 2 as Detective Rogue Kelly from New York to investigate a series of biblical plagues terrorizing Music City. This has led many people to hope that a crossover could be coming, as Hewitt, his former co-star from I Know What You Did Last Summer, is on 9-1-1. Fans are finally getting their wish, because Hewitt has posted an Instagram video from the set of 9-1-1, joined by Phillippe, and it’s literally everything:

A post shared by Jennifer Love Hewitt (@jenniferlovehewitt)

It shouldn’t be too much of a surprise that the two are working together. Not only has ABC been making occasional references to the horror hit on social media, but Phillippe was recently asked about reuniting with Hewitt. He teased that “maybe” it’s going to happen, and I’m really glad that “maybe” turned into “definitely.” Because the 9-1-1s are heading into their fall finales next week, fans will have to wait until the new year for this reunion, but the wait will definitely be worth it. I cannot wait to see Rogue and Maddie interacting with each other.

As for what could possibly take Rogue to LA, details have not been shared. However, the homicide detective previously revealed that he has two sons, one of whom lives in LA. It’s entirely possible that he could be in the city to visit his son, and he gets wrapped up in a case. Or something work-related will bring him to the City of Angels. As long as the potential case doesn’t involve his son, because that would be gut-wrenching, and he interacts with Maddie a lot, I’m all for it.

With 9-1-1 and Nashville filming across the country from each other, I’ve been wondering just how many in-person crossovers the franchise would be able to do. Oliver Stark and Ryan Guzman managed to make it to Nashville last season for a fun crossover, and I’m glad that Phillippe is going to LA this season. Whether more 9-1-1: Nashville characters could follow him is unclear, or vice versa, but the 113 and 118 are still in contact with each other. Buck even helped out the 113 on FaceTime earlier this season on 9-1-1: Nashville to help with an emergency that called back to the 9-1-1 pilot.

At the very least, I could not be happier that the 9-1-1s are taking advantage of having two stars from I Know What You Did Last Summer on their shows. And even though I have no clue what is going to happen in that episode, I am so excited. For now, though, fans will have to settle for the fall finales of 9-1-1 and 9-1-1: Nashville, airing on Thursday beginning at 8 p.m. ET on ABC, and streaming the next day with a Hulu subscription.

#3492. These Bose QuietComfort Headphones Are $160 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3491. 20 Years Later, A Classic Nintendo DS Puzzle Game Officially Returns

20 years later, Professor Layton’s Nintendo DS debut is getting a remake

Next year will mark the 20th anniversary of Level-5's beloved Professor Layton series. To celebrate, the company has announced it is remaking Professor Layton and the Curious Village.

Level-5 announced the remake with a teaser trailer on its YouTube channel. Professor Layton and the Curious Village was first released in 2007 on the Nintendo DS handheld, with a global release bringing the game to a wider audience the following year. It debuted the series' signature puzzle-solving mechanics while introducing players to the titular hero and his apprentice, Luke Triton. It was met with widespread acclaim upon its release and launched a series that is still going strong nearly 20 years later.

The game sees Layton and Luke exploring the village of St. Mystere in search of the Golden Apple. A recently deceased baron declares that whoever finds the mysterious artifact will inherit his fortune, and the residents help the leading duo along while also engaging them in a series of puzzles.

Beyond the 2027 release window, Level-5 hasn't shared a specific release date. For what it's worth, the original game released on Feb. 15, 2007, so perhaps we could be looking at a February launch. The remake has been confirmed for Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Windows PC.

The remake looks to be in the same style as the upcoming Professor Layton and the New World of Steam. The teaser site highlights the remake's new 3D rendering and high-resolution. While not confirmed, it is possible Professor Layton and the Curious Village will include the use of generative AI in some way, as Level-5 has gone on record in defense of technology in game development. Professor Layton and the New World of Steam is the first original title in the series since 2013.

Level-5 will finally deliver Professor Layton and the New World of Steam in 2026

#3490. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3489. 37 Years Later, Dolly Parton's Steel Magnolias Line Is Still The Greatest Quote On Grief

"Steel Magnolias" is one of those movies that always seems to be perpetually playing on television, not unlike the Best Picture Oscar-winning "Forrest Gump." Both movies also take place in the South, depicting the trials and tribulations of characters in small towns as they confront the challenges of life, love, and loss.

But whereas "Forrest Gump" follows a single man on his journey across touchstones of the history of the U.S., "Steel Magnolias" keeps the story isolated to a group of women played by Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis, Julia Roberts, and the late Dolly Parton. Directed by Herbert Ross and written by Robert Harling, based on his own 1987 stage play of the same name, the film is both tragic and funny as we follow the ups, downs, and in-betweens of these charming and occasionally sassy ladies.

Critics were mixed on the movie, with Hal Hinson of The Washington Post writing that the film "runs on gags, pitched to the cheapest seats, and maudlin emotion, pitched to the cheapest sentiments. The script [...] is on a degenerated line from Tennessee Williams by way of Hallmark cards." Meanwhile, Roger Ebert praised the movie, writing, "'Steel Magnolias' is essentially a series of comic one-liners leading up to a teary tragedy, but let it be said that the one-liners are mostly funny and the tragedy deserves most, but not all, of the tears."

The laughter and the tears are exactly why we're talking about "Steel Magnolias" now, as it's full of delightful quips and barbs alongside sentiments that might feel like greeting card schmaltz but still pack charm and an emotional punch. That's especially the case when it comes to one of Parton's memorable lines as Truvy Jones, the owner of a home-salon where the Southern women frequently congregate.

One of the driving forces of "Steel Magnolias" is Julia Roberts as Shelby Eatenton-Latcherie, a role for which she earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Shelby has type 1 diabetes, which turns her hope for having children into a health risk. Sadly, as Shelby pursues her motherly desire, the pregnancy damages her kidneys, and she's forced to go on dialysis. But Shelby's mother, Mary Lynn "M'Lynn" Eatenton (Sally Field) is able to donate a kidney to help save her from further grief.

Unfortunately, Shelby dies due to an infection caused by the suppressive therapy that keeps her body from rejecting the kidney. Stuck unconscious in a hospital, Shelby's family makes the difficult decision to take her off life support.

After the funeral, M'Lynn is overwhelmed. In a burst of emotion, she swings dramatically through pain, anger, sadness, and disbelief, but then there's a bit of laughter. M'Lynn expresses that she "just wants to hit somebody" until they feel as bad as she does. That's when M'Lynn's friend Clairee Belcher (Olympia Dukakis) offers up Louisa "Ouiser" Boudreaux (Shirley Maclaine) for M'Lynn to punch, much to Ouiser's disbelief and the shock of the other women. It's a hilarious moment that eases the tension and offers some relief.

In the aftermath, M'Lynn apologizes for her emotional outburst, but Truvy offers consolation by saying:

"Laughter through tears is my favorite emotion."

You can see the Hallmark-tinged vibe of a line like that, but being cheesy doesn't make it any less true. In the shadow of tragedy, laughing through tears offers a welcome break from the exhaustion of grief. After the death of a loved one, you may even find yourself making dark jokes to cope with the sadness and anger that you feel, and that's okay. You don't have to laugh to keep from crying. Instead, you can laugh through the tears.

Here are some other memorable quotes from "Steel Magnolias," each with its own charm:

"Smile! It increases your face value." — Truvy Jones

"Well, you know what they say: if you don't have anything nice to say about anybody, come sit by me!" — Clairee Belcher

"I'm not crazy, I've just been in a very bad mood 40 years!" — Ouiser Boudreaux

"Honey, time marches on, and eventually, you realize it is marchin' across your face." — Truvy Jones

"The only thing that separates us from the animals is our ability to accessorize." — Clairee Belcher

"I would rather have 30 minutes of wonderful than a lifetime of nothing special." — Shelby Eatenton-Latcherie

"A dirty mind is a terrible thing to waste." — Ouiser Boudreaux

"I have a strict policy that nobody cries alone in my presence." — Truvy Jones

1976’s Rocky may be 50 years old now, but the franchise, powered by Sylvester Stallone’s iconic character, has proven to be as durable as the fighter himself. In total, there have been nine entries so far in the Rocky franchise (six Rocky movies and three Creed movies), and that doesn’t include I Am Rocky, the biopic about Stallone making first movie made, which hits the 2026 movie schedule this month.

In a recent interview with Andy Cohen on Cohen’s SiriusXM channel, the host asked Stallone which of the five sequels (not including the original movie) was his favorite, and I have to admit I didn’t expect one of them. Here’s how Stallone answered the original question:

It's II and VI for me. II because that's when he gets married. That's when he really, like, wins. It's very, very potent.

That he loves Rocky II isn’t really a surprise. Though I don’t think it’s quite as good as the original, I do think it’s a really great follow-up. Stallone obviously hones in on how personal it is for the character, a character he certainly feels a kinship with. Getting married to Adrian (Talia Shire) is a big moment in the franchise. Yes, the Rocky movies are boxing movies, but they are just as much about Rocky and Adrian’s relationship from their courtship in the original, through her tragic death before the events of Rocky Balboa (VI).

That makes Stallone’s second choice for a favorite a clear choice. It is the one that surprised me, but it makes perfect sense. The sixth movie in the franchise (and the first not to have an actual number attached) is a movie about aging, loss, and death. It picks up many years after the events of Rocky V. Rocky is retired from boxing and now owns a restaurant in his hometown of Philadelphia. Here’s what makes it special, according to Stallone:

And then Rocky VI, it deals with something that everyone deals with, which is grief and the loss and how he's talking to his child about, 'I held you here, you were the greatest thing, and now.' It's not how hard you hit, you know, it's about life. So, it was very poignant that – I love that movie. That was some of my best writing by far.

I agree with Stallone that Rocky Balboa is some of his best writing (outside of the original). It was such an interesting way to bring the character full circle. It starts with his love for Adrian and ends with him dealing with the loss of his beloved wife. It’s also about family relationships, specifically with their son, Robert Jr. (Milo Ventimiglia), and how they shift and ebb and flow over the years. Rocky Balboa gets the series back to its roots after, let's be honest, so many more cartoonish entries. I LOVE Rocky IV, but it doesn’t have the emotional depth of I, II, or VI, and let’s not even talk about Rocky V.

You can celebrate all the Rocky movies this month, either for the release of I Am Rocky, or for Rocky’s 50th anniversary with a Prime subscription, where they are all available.

#3487. New Friday The 13th Movie Is Finally Happening, With A Familiar Director

Jason lives! After nearly 20 years, Jason Voorhees is finally returning to the big screen in what will be (appropriately enough) the 13th film in the "Friday the 13th" franchise. The rights to the "Friday the 13th" series have been stuck in a bit of a legal mess over the years, but according to an official press release from Horror, Inc., a new film is in the works — with a familiar filmmaker at the helm. Steve Miner, who directed "Friday the 13th Part 2" and "Friday the 13th Part III" (which was the first movie to give Jason his now-iconic hockey mask) will direct this new entry.

Some fans will no doubt love that Jason is back on the big screen in any form, while more cynical folks (like me, for instance) will wonder if this is little more than an attempt to cling onto the complicated rights to a well-established franchise. Miner hasn't directed a movie in a while, and it might have been a bit more exciting to hand the reins over to a fresh new director with new ideas. Then again, it's not like these movies need to be complicated. We just want to see Jason hack and slash. In any case, the new "Friday the 13th" comes on the heels of "Crystal Lake," the TV series that served as an origin story for Jason and his killer mother.

Per the press release, Horror, Inc., under the leadership of the Barsamian family, will finance and produce the film, with CatchLight Studios as a production partner, and Cineverse securing North America distribution rights. David Fliegel will pen the script. Per Fleigel's IMDb page, this will apparently be his first produced screenplay. His only other credits are for producing and "additional crew."

The last time Jason was up on the big screen was in 2009's "Friday the 13th" reboot, which was a box office hit but did not spawn a whole new franchise as intended. Since then, the series has languished in a legal quagmire, with Jason only returning in a short film (titled "Sweet Revenge") and the aforementioned "Crystal Lake" series.

As a kid who grew up haunting the horror section of the video store, I'm always up for some new Jason action, and it does seem crazy that we haven't had a new "Friday the 13th" movie in so long. Still, I can't help but think something seems a bit off about this announcement. But hey, I'm hoping for the best. Jason has survived space, New York City, and Freddy Krueger. He's a resilient guy. I'm pulling for him.

#3486. 25 Years Later, Frodo’s Best Lord of the Ring Quote Proves He's the Ultimate Fantasy Hero

An inherent tragedy follows every character in The Lord of the Rings, which isn’t surprising, given that Peter Jackson’s epic fantasy trilogy is adapted from the works of J.R.R. Tolkien. The author has never been shy about exploring grim topics, and in a 1968 interview with the BBC, Tolkien said that all stories are about one thing: death.

Though grim, Tolkien’s perspective is not necessarily mistaken. His sentiments also emerge through the characters in his stories, including Frodo Baggins, first introduced in The Fellowship of the Ring. Through Frodo’s struggle to carry the One Ring to the fires of Mount Doom, Tolkien’s outlook is reflected in how his characters confront hardship and life’s darker aspects.

Hardship often invites self-reflection when a quiet moment offers the chance to look back. Across The Lord of the Rings trilogy, characters both minor and central reflect on the events that shaped their respective journeys. Frodo, in particular, experiences several moments of introspection throughout the story, as he considers the weight of his quest and the changes it has brought.

However, one moment stands apart: a poignant quote in which he lets his vulnerability show, a line that has remained with fans of Peter Jackson’s trilogy for decades.

Though Frodo delivers many memorable lines throughout The Lord of the Rings, one stands out for its brevity and profound resonance. In just a few words, it captures the immense burden of his quest and the sacrifices he must make along the way.

During a quiet moment in the shadowy, foreboding Mines of Moria, where the Fellowship entered after their route over the Misty Mountains was blocked, Frodo seeks solace and reassurance from Gandalf.

In just a few short words, Frodo’s best quote reveals the exact headspace the young hobbit is in. He says:

“I wish the ring had never come to me. I wish none of this had happened.”

Because Frodo says this so early in his journey, it's easy to dismiss his attitude. After all, we know in hindsight that his real struggles are only just beginning. In fact, things become much more difficult for him and the rest of the Fellowship almost immediately after he says this.

Dismissing Frodo’s words as mere childish sulking willfully misreads why the young Hobbit is so forlorn in the first place.

Fans should remember that Frodo and his fellow hobbits (Samwise, Merry, and Pippin) grew up in the Shire, a peaceful community largely untouched by strife and malice. Their lives there were far removed from the dangers and conflicts of the wider world, so setting off on a perilous adventure would have seemed extraordinary.

Even Bilbo Baggins, Frodo’s uncle, was viewed as reckless when he left the Shire to join Gandalf and Thorin’s company of 12 dwarves on a quest to reclaim Erebor and its treasure from the dragon Smaug. Bilbo’s adventure was not regarded as an example to follow, but as an unusually risky departure from the safe and familiar life the hobbits knew.

With that context in mind, Frodo’s words to Gandalf make a lot of sense. He’s a fish out of water, still wrestling with the fact that, because his uncle Bilbo left the One Ring to him, he must now face a destiny far bigger than himself.

Moreover, Frodo cannot simply walk away from his mission without putting the rest of Middle-earth at risk. The One Ring’s influence follows him throughout the trilogy, constantly tempting him to give in to its power.

Yet Frodo is not the only one vulnerable to its pull: even his most steadfast allies, including Aragorn, are not immune. If someone as resolute as Aragorn can be tempted by the Ring, Frodo has little choice but to shoulder the burden himself. He must keep carrying it, knowing its power could endanger anyone who tries to take it from him — at least until Sam arrives and helps him bear the weight of the journey.

Frodo’s task is neither joyful nor one he would have chosen. He isn’t a hero seeking an adventure like his uncle. He is a hobbit burdened by a quest to save the world, because he is the only one who can. By accepting his responsibility to the rest of the Fellowship and continuing despite not wanting to, Frodo proves he is the perfect hero.

#3485. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

Elijah Wood, of course, famously starred in three of The Lord of the Rings movies, so you’d think returning to play Frodo Baggins would be something like going home. Wood can’t gush enough about getting to be in Hunt for Gollum, but it turns out reprising the role came with its own surprises for the actor as well.

The Hunt for Gollum is on the 2027 movie schedule for the holiday season, and the production recently wrapped filming in New Zealand. Here’s what Wood had to say about returning to play the beloved Hobbit:

And I think one of the things that I hadn't anticipated because, I don't know that we're that self-aware because we were the ones who were a part of the making of the thing. But this many years on, the crew is now largely younger people, and they all grew up on these films. And that's a whole other element that I just didn't even think about.

The first Lord of the Rings movie came out back in 2001, making the movie franchise 25 years old this year. While it might have felt like no time had passed for the actor when he returned to The Shire, being back on set, he realized that these films have inspired an entire generation of fans. As he added to Deadline:

But there's a reverence for these movies. We just made them. Of course, we revere them, but we're the ones that made them. So that was a whole other element that was quite surprising, and something I hadn't really anticipated. Just the reverence for those movies and those characters and seeing Gandalf walk in the set was like an awe-inspiring moment for people who had grown to watch those movies. So that was really cool and very sweet.

To be honest, I’m a little surprised that Wood didn’t think about this. I imagine he’s being approached all the time by people who love The Lord of the Rings movies and want to tell him about it. But apparently being on set with a whole new group of crew members really put things into perspective, as he also said this about the experience:

It was beautiful and surreal, and it felt like no time had passed, and it felt like stepping back into time. You know, looking down at my [feet and] having this sort of muscle memory of like, 'I've seen these feet this way. I know this wardrobe.' That feeling is so wild. It's so transportive. It's like suddenly 27 years are gone, and you're back in it again. So that was really lovely and special.

Wow, it sounds like it was really something special for the original Lord of the Rings actor.

Elijah Wood returns to the franchise alongside Andy Serkis, who will star as Gollum and is the feature's director, Ian McKellen, who will play Gandalf again and Lee Pace, who is back as Thranduil.

Also, Jamie Dornan is taking over the role of Aragorn, which he recently said he “cried” over when he got the part. Anya Taylor-Joy is playing an elf, because of course she is, and both Kate Winslet and Leo Woodall have been cast in key roles, too.

Elijah Wood has called The Hunt for Gollum “a side quest” in The Lord of the Rings universe since it’s not directly based on any of J.R.R. Tolkien’s novels. You can check out the first look at the movie that Serkis revealed during production below:

A post shared by The Lord of the Rings (@lordoftherings)

In the video, you can catch a first glimpse of the back of Elijah Wood’s Frodo opening a door. I don’t know about you, but I’m feeling all warm and fuzzy thinking about seeing Frodo again, and it sounds like there were a lot of positive feelings for the actor while he was back in New Zealand making the movie. Its release date, December 17, 2027, can’t come soon enough!

While we wait, we can look forward to seeing Elijah Wood in the final season of Yellowjackets, which premieres on November 20. And the Lord of the Rings TV series, Rings of Power, just premiered its first batch of episodes this week, with more on the way for the next two Wednesdays over on Amazon Prime.

#3483. How To Rob A Bank Director David Leitch Reveals His Favorite Scene In The Movie [Exclusive]

Warning: This article contains light spoilers for "How to Rob a Bank."

David Leitch doesn't make things easy, and that's entirely by design. Of course, it's little surprise that the director behind punchy, stunt-centric movies like "The Fall Guy" or "Atomic Blonde" would opt for a more deliberate approach rather than the simplest one. His latest, "How to Rob a Bank," is just the latest in that trend. The unconventional, genre-redefining heist flick almost immediately makes a choice to embrace its own way of doing things — in this case, using a content creator aesthetic as star Nicholas Hoult's main protagonist Ryan (aka The Wolf) and his criminal crew go viral with their DIY social media channel. But how do you take that over-the-top stylistic direction and make it work alongside a much more grounded, emotional, and politically relevant storyline?

Fortunately, I had the chance to ask Leitch about how he pulled this off in "How to Rob a Bank" during a recent press junket. As it turns out, balancing two such divergent tones presented its own unique problem that had to be solved creatively. For Leitch, it was a matter of delineating between both aspects of writer Mark Bianculli's script and having form follow function:

"There were two very different visual stories we were telling. We were telling the grounded story of these characters and their very relatable plights that are happening, that are a snapshot of our times. And we shot that on 35 millimeter and there was a very traditional visual style we chose intentionally for that. Then you had these bombastic episodes of this charismatic content creator. And then the challenge was bringing those two worlds together. Actually, the challenge opportunity was exciting to bring them together."

In fact, Leitch pinpoints the moment where these worlds finally collide.

As much as "How to Rob a Bank" presents itself as a rollicking, thrill-a-minute roller coaster ride, things take an abrupt turn an hour in. Our gang of bank-robbing Robin Hoods make a key mistake, their dogged pursuers (led by Zoë Kravitz's tech-wiz Reagan and John C. Reilly's FBI Agent John West) track down their identities, and they soon land on opposite sides of an interrogation room. But, as the leader of this pack, Ryan has never found a setback he can't turn into a teachable moment — or, more cynically, a piece of content.

That's exactly what happens here, when both halves of the movie come into focus. "I think where we do it really well, and it's my favorite scene in the movie," David Leitch explains to me, "is during the interrogation sequence, where we're blurring the lines between the Wolf's show — basically [explaining] how to survive an interrogation — and the actual footage, being in the real interrogation." Here, Leitch and his creative team splice together straightforward imagery from the interrogation (which is mostly our defiant characters sitting silently, demanding their lawyer) and imagery where Ryan uses (or imagines?) this as his latest YouTube video: How to Survive an Interrogation.

According to Leitch, this allowed him to play with what we're seeing versus what's really happening:

"Even the characters in the movie breaking the fourth wall or texts coming up on the screen when we're in the film, now it's like [the] content creator visual style is changing the way that I'm telling you the narrative aspect of the film. And I'm actually using the narrative aspect of the film to influence the way that I composed the content creator footage."

Despite the complexity in putting this sequence together, all of this is seamlessly cut and presented in a way where it hardly even registers to moviegoers. At the moment, we're too concerned with the fate of Ryan, his lover Emi (Anna Sawai), and the rest of their friends as all their best-laid plans come crashing down. Adding to the tension is the delicate balance of power suddenly shifting away from these honorable thieves trying to make a societal point and towards the man representing all the structural ills they're fighting against: FBI Agent John West.

During our conversation, "How to Rob a Bank" producer and 87North production company founder Kelly McCormick chimes in and adds, "That's exactly where the power is shifting and where the worlds are colliding. So, in a masterful way, [David Leitch is] toying with you there, manipulating you with both ways of storytelling." Intriguingly, none of this is meant to register to viewers who are (hopefully) absorbed by the storytelling in the moment. According to Leitch, this is something that he only conveyed through the subtext and through the visuals in how he and director of photography Jonathan Sela shot the scene:

"It's not necessary for the audience to really understand it, but that's the uneasy feeling I'm trying to give, is the power switching."

We won't give away anything that happens next, but it's safe to say this is the turning point where things kick into another gear. From that point on, the film's stakes are firmly set and nobody feels safe. "How to Rob a Bank" is now playing in theaters.

When you’re responsible for wiping out half the universe, people are going to keep bringing it up. So obviously, most fan questions Josh Brolin gets asked have to do with Thanos, especially from curious minds who want to know if the Titan will ever return. However, the actor was recently asked about an entirely different character in the Marvel universe. Now, I’m aware that Brolin still has love for Thanos, but the real question is: Would he ever come back as Deadpool 2’s Cable?

With the upcoming X-Men reboot, people want to know if we’ll be seeing him again. So while promoting his new survival thriller Whalefall at NYCC, The Direct asked what the likelihood of seeing Cable again is, and Brolin revealed:

Thanos to me is a very, very interesting role, and a role that I had a lot of fun doing. You know what I mean? A lot of fun doing. Joe Russo, Anthony Russo, those guys to me, they're just unprecedented, unparalleled... There's some practicality to it, but when you resort to your imagination, and they would come up and they would reference Scarface or something like that, something that I understood, then it made it even better. 'Deadpool 2', I'm glad happened. I'm glad [Cable] was isolated unto that experience, and it's a good memory.

In the movie, the character is a time-traveling anti-hero who was also the son of Scott Summers and a clone of Jean Grey. Some ‘timey-wimey’ stuff later, and he’s back in the present after living in a dystopian future. With various X-Men, including James Marsden as Cyclops, coming back, it makes sense that people want to know about Cable. However, it sounds like Brolin is happy to leave that character in the past. Although Deadpool creator Rob Liefeld has shared that he thinks there’s “much more meat on those bones” when it comes to Cable.

So, hear me out. In the spirit of reboots, they could cast a younger Cable and do an origin story as part of a grander X-Men plot. We have Mister Sinister in the upcoming reboot, which could lead to a Jean clone, and this could bring the story full circle to Cable earlier in his journey. Now that there’s a mergence of the mutant characters with our MCU, anything is technically possible.

While Brolin’s time as Cable seems to be “isolated” in the past, that doesn’t mean his time as the Mad Titan is over forever. The actor has shared that if the Russo Brothers ever asked, then he’d be open to returning. So maybe if the right person asked, he'd return (even for just a cameo) as Cable one day.

While we're all still thinking about his Marvel work, Brolin has been hard at work outside of the MCU. In addition to Whalefall in October, the actor also had The Dog Stars out this year, which he described as one of the “more creative, satisfying” projects he’s been part of. He also has a role in Dune: Part 3, which hits the 2026 schedule on December 18 alongside Avengers: Doomsday.

So even though we won't be seeing Cable or Thanos anytime soon, you can go see him reprise his role as Gurney Halleck in Dune.

#3481. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3480. Johnny Depp's Ebenezer Makes An Alarming Change To The Story Of A Christmas Carol

When the ads and pre-release buzz articles began running for "Ebenezer," the new film directed by Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge, the campaign promised that the movie would present Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol" as you'd never seen it before. Yet, now that the film has released and folks (including yours truly) have screened it, it turns out "Ebenezer" is unsurprisingly more or less the same "A Christmas Carol" we all know well. The movie liberally copy-and-pastes whole swathes of Dickens' text into the script, with writer Nathaniel Halpern even bothering to include the novella's separation into five staves. However, it seems there's some larger artistic liberty wiggle room in that "more or less the same" than might appear at first glance.

When West spoke to Entertainment Weekly back in August, he detailed what made Depp's Ebenezer different than previous adaptations. Amidst talking up things like Depp's "musicality" as a performer, West also explained how his film would present Scrooge in a more both sides-y manner: "As [Depp's] Scrooge cuts someone down verbally or as he makes a financial point or withdraws, you do understand why he's doing it." That offhand mention of "a financial point" baffled many of us when we first read it, as it certainly did sound like a deviation from Dickens.

Was this Scrooge going to be portrayed as a genius businessman? Instead, the changes "Ebenezer" makes to Scrooge and Dickens' story are of a smaller nature. They involve portraying a couple small supporting characters as outright villains, thereby giving Scrooge a justification for his misanthropy. The changes may be merely tweaks, yet their larger implications are alarming, especially for a film which doesn't feel able to support them.

For the most part, "Ebenezer" is a faithful adaptation of "A Christmas Carol." The largest addition comes in the form of a prologue in which we see Scrooge and his partner, Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen), on their last day together. Marley goes to get some tea while Scrooge observes a beggar outside his window. At the same moment the beggar reveals himself to Scrooge as a fraud conning people out of their donations, Marley drops dead, equating the con artist's crime with harm done to a true earner in Scrooge's mind. That Marley (and Scrooge) are just as heartless and dishonest is something the film hopes Dickens' work gets across, as they don't go out of their way to underline it to support their addition.

This problem is compounded twice. Once is when it's revealed that Scrooge's old benevolent boss Fezziwig was murdered by a street beggar, further teaching Scrooge that charity can be met with violence. Next is when the Ghost of Christmas Future shows Scrooge the vultures who've come to sully his legacy after his death, which adds the wrinkle that the two men who sought a donation for the poor at the beginning of the film are actually also embezzlers.

What's more, they're in league with a man who's plotting with the embezzlers to steal Scrooge's nephew Fred's inheritance with the production of a forged will. The alarming quality about these inclusions lies in how they seem to give Scrooge more moral justification for his odious behavior that he doesn't need. It's a bizarrely tone-deaf addition for a story that's ultimately meant to be about the virtues of charity.

Ultimately (and thankfully), these additions do not derail "Ebenezer," for the heart of Charles Dickens' story and his themes remains intact. Although it's tempting to point fingers at the Skydance corporation for the new ideas, it isn't the changes themselves that are the problem. After all, Ti West comes from a background of indie horror films, many of which utilize thorny, morally ambiguous characterizations and themes as their stock in trade. "Ebenezer" is indeed partially constructed to emphasize the horror in Dickens' tale: the three Christmas ghosts are more ghastly and doomed than they typically are. In the more horror-centric version of "A Christmas Carol" the movie seems to want to be, a somewhat justified Scrooge would be a fascinating layer for an actor to play, as it creates a new obstacle for the character to overcome on his journey to selflessness.

Alas, "Ebenezer" is the Johnny Depp show, and for several reasons, Depp is not up to the task. While it's arguable that he may not be able to tackle such material at all, it seems like he's not even interested in trying in the first place. Instead, "Ebenezer" and Depp are too preoccupied with trying to be as likable as possible, which means that his Scrooge rarely gets nasty. He comes off more like an irritable jerk than a man who's nearly lost his soul, so whatever compelling shadings the changes to the story could've presented never materialize. On paper, the possibilities presented by "Ebenezer" range from exciting to alarming. Yet we needn't fret too much, since the finished film plays things so safely that it's hard to get riled up about it one way or the other.

#3479. How To Rob A Bank Director Reveals The Real-Life Inspirations Behind The Movie's Influencers [Exclusive]

Of all the movies in 2026 that can claim to be the timeliest, none may have a better case than "How to Rob a Bank." Even setting aside the obvious social and political commentary behind director David Leitch's newest heist flick, in which a group of Robin Hood-like bank robbers team up to send a message to corporate bigwigs and capitalist vultures, the movie's timeliness is also apparent in the way it's shot and edited. The various trailers have made no secret of the content creator angle behind this crew, led by Nicholas Hoult's Ryan (aka The Wolf). When they're not sticking up banks and making thrilling getaways, they're busy editing their escapades into viral-ready YouTube videos to be consumed by the masses.

It's a novel approach that'll either work or not for audiences, many of whom are well aware of the online ecosystem that is influencer culture. It's a tall task for any mainstream Hollywood movie to tackle, but the creative team behind "How to Rob a Bank" clearly did their homework. During a recent press junket for the film, I spoke to both Leitch and producing partner Kelly McCormick about the deep well of influences they drew from in order to nail this specific element of the film — one that certainly attempts to feel true to our digital lives. According to McCormick:

"We were trying to go for what might be the next push for creators, if you know what I mean. Like, the wish fulfillment aspect from a creator's perspective of just pushing the envelope even more. So it was just really absorbing as much as possible to see what was out there and then using some of the prosumer cameras to make sure that we were just being even more wild."

The content creator footage depicted throughout "How to Rob a Bank" will inevitably leave an impression. No, we don't live in a world where adrenaline-seeking influencers actually put themselves and others in harm's way to pull off successful heists and robberies. (Not yet, at least.) But actually capturing those vibes in an authentic way meant resorting to some very specific filmmaking measures.

One scene shows Ryan and his friends fleeing the scene of the crime on motorcycles through a forest, with GoPros strapped to their helmets capturing footage in every direction. When this is filtered through the lens of the video they upload afterwards, well, that's where things get visually dynamic. As Kelly McCormick explained to me:

"The one [scene] in specific I always remember is when they're biking through the forest and you see it from above and we are pivoting the camera in editorial, because literally it's capturing [360 degrees] around [the action]. And so you can spin it around in editorial to get that vibe of this wild editing that I think would be a creator's dream, if they didn't have to hit deadlines and always be feeding as much as possible to their hungry, hungry followers [laughs]."

David Leitch name-checks "extreme sports" as one section of YouTube they paid particular attention to for sequences like that, while the idea of philanthropy and giving back to communities was taken out of the Mr. Beast playbook. Even podcasters get into the mix, like Scott Galloway or King Bach (both of whom make cameos in the film). Adds Leitch with a laugh, "We had a lot of influences in our influencers."

#3478. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

With the new Harry Potter series getting closer, Daniel Radcliffe has been getting a lot of questions about any advice he has for Dominic McLaughlin. The actor has previously said he didn’t have advice for McLaughlin and only shared advice for the producers. At the time, he asked them to “let [the young cast] be kids still,” especially in the age of social media. However, I was surprised by his take on why he doesn’t want to give advice.

While the actor was promoting his upcoming movie, Steps, he was asked by AP News Entertainment about handing down the wand. The actor doubled down on not sharing advice, but this time he explained why:

I’m really, truly in the business of not giving Dominic advice. He’s got it, he doesn’t need any advice from me. I don’t want to be like a — because then if I say something to you, then the next interview [with him], people will be like, ‘Oh, Dan said you should do this.’ And I don’t want to haunt this poor child through interviews.

It’s understandable that he doesn’t want to put even more on McLaughlin’s shoulders. It’s a little surprising, though I can see why he doesn’t want to put the young actor under pressure to live up to anything. Meanwhile, he’s not the only Harry Potter actor who has been asked to hand down advice. Bonnie Wright, who played Ginny Weasley, shares a similar opinion to Radcliffe when it comes to telling the next Ginny what to do. She has stated, “I think it’s so important for them to be in their world and their interpretation of it.”

This seems to be largely what the original cast thinks, with Tom Felton also veering away from giving advice on how to portray Draco. However, the Broadway actor focused on the sentimentality of his Harry Potter days and advises the new cast to take lots of pictures. It seems that Radcliffe isn’t the only one not wishing to ‘haunt’ the child actors. Though this take on advice is a little surprising, Radcliffe’s reveal that he’s not a big TV watcher is even more so:

I don’t know if I will [watch] honestly. I’ve been in a lot of Harry Potter already and also, not even because I don’t — I don’t watch any TV. I haven’t seen Breaking Bad, and I haven’t seen Mad Men. I haven’t seen some of the real classics. Eight hours is a lot of anything to watch.

I’m not surprised he hasn’t watched his own franchise, but he’s so behind on so many classics. Perhaps he’ll check out the Harry Potter series with his son. Hopefully, after Season 1 airs, someone will ask him. Though I doubt watching the series will change his stance on giving advice.

Meanwhile, this hasn’t stopped a few of his co-stars. Ralph Fiennes gave some practical advice to whoever takes his place as Voldemort: “Practice your long, flowing, robe walk” and advised him not to trip. Additionally, a pair of Weasleys have shared the sweet gesture they gave to the next Fred and George, up-and-coming actors Tristan and Gabriel Harland. Oliver and James Phelps sent the twins sweet notes wishing the next set of mischief makers the best of luck. They declined to give exact details about what was in the notes, stating they were private messages of encouragement.

The Harry Potter series will arrive on the TV schedule on Christmas Day. It is expected to have a weekly release and will be available with an HBO Max subscription.

#3475. How to get Go Safari Balls in Pokémon Go

These high catch rate balls will help you grab rare Pokémon quickly

These high catch rate balls will help you grab rare Pokémon quickly

You can get Go Safari Balls as part of Pokémon Go Wild Area events, and can only be used during event hours. No, seriously — they disappear after the event ends.

These balls are based off of the regular camouflaged-print Safari Balls from the mainline games. Usually, you can only use Safari Balls in the Safari Zone, a special area where wild Pokémon roam and you can’t actually battle them. You can throw treats and rocks at them to try to increase their catch rate, but ultimately, you just had to huck Safari Balls at them to catch some of these rare critters.

Pokémon Go has its own take on Safari Balls, and we explain what Go Safari Balls do, and how to get more.

Go Safari Balls are special Poké Balls that have a higher catch rate. While the catch rate isn’t 100% known, it is known to be much better than an Ultra Ball.

They are particularly effective against "mighty Pokémon", which also debut as part of the Go Wild Area event, but know you can use them for anything. This includes Galarian birds, which have a notoriously low catch rate, so make sure to use your Daily Adventure Incense during the event period to increase your chances if you haven’t got them yet.

For those with a paid Go Wild Area ticket, during the raid’s catch phase, Premier Balls will also be swapped out for Go Safari Balls in raids and Max Battles — but know any leftovers will be discarded and not kept for other encounters.

Remember, these are an event exclusive ball and will disappear at the end of the event on Sunday, Nov. 15 — so be sure to use them before 6 p.m. in your local time on Sunday rolls round.

Pokémon caught in Go Safari Balls can be transferred to Pokémon Home, but the appearance of the ball is changed into a greenish "Strange Ball" once transferred.

There are a few ways to get more Go Safari Balls during the event, though not very many options for players looking to avoid spending. That being said, you’ll want to start playing early to complete the research if you want to get and use your allotment of Go Safari Balls before they vanish.

Note that even the paid balls will disappear on Sunday, Nov. 15 at 6 p.m. in your local time, so make sure you use them up.
