#3443. Ghost Soldier Ending Explained: How Jim Caviezel's New Action Hero Destroys Brownstone

In 2023, actor Jim Caviezel (best known for playing Jesus Christ in Mel Gibson’s The Passion of the Christ) starred in Angel Studios’ Sound of Freedom. The film was a surprise smash hit at the box office and with audiences, putting Angel Studios on the map. Sound of Freedom earned over $250 million on a meager $15 million production budget, proving to be one of the most profitable films of the year. Now, he's back with another movie — Ghost Soldier, which premiered this week for a Veteran's Day release.

Sound of Freedom may have had just a 57% score critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, but it was still a huge hit with audiences. The Alejandro Monteverde-directed action epic earned a whopping 99% audience score on the site, highlighting just how much viewers connected with the film. That’s in spite of the political controversy and general divisiveness that the movie generated too. As a result, many have high expectations for Ghost Soldier.

It’s no surprise, then, that Jim Caviezel is back in another action film that embraces many of the same themes and values as Sound of Freedom. In the new film, Caviezel plays a former special operatives soldier who is forced to protect his town from a villainous corporation seeking to displace residents from their homes in order to build a cooling plant for AI data centers.

Ghost Soldier is described as a faith-based action film, and one that is being released on Veterans Day because of the military themes present throughout. Caviezel’s Henry Fitzgerald isn’t the only character to have served in the military, and the film shows how the action follows Fitz even after he departed the service. All of this builds up to a jam-packed finale, and one that puts Fitz in grave danger as he pushes back against the company and its third party mercenaries.

At the heart of this story is a villainous company called the Brownstone Corporation. The fictional company is deeply involved in artificial intelligence and is led by foreign investors based in the Middle East. Blackstone is said to have invested significant amounts of money in new artificial intelligence data centers and are intent on ensuring their long-term success.

Fitz defeats Brownstone with a meticulous plan, and one that begins long before the grand finale. For starters, he goes to the home of the Brownstone lawyer that accompanied their mercenaries to the Hernandez residence and uses threats of torture to coerce useful information out of her. What's more, he lays the groundwork for the company's downfall by convincing her to take what she knows to the press.

However, a lot more is needed in order to take down Brownstone. Fitz recognizes this, and opts to use his many advanced weapons in battle against the company’s mercenaries. One of these weapons is a cloak of invisibility, something that feels as if it’s been pulled straight from the wizarding world of Harry Potter.

Fitz uses this cloak, along with his many other weapons, as he infiltrates a Brownstone party, held to celebrate their recent successes and the launch of their plans. Fitz poses as a waiter initially, but quickly attracts the attention of security, and it’s at this moment that the fighting begins. Fitz fends off countless soldiers, and eventually uses explosives to destroy the cooling center that Browstone had been building, thus crushing the company’s plans in the region. He also uses missiles to destroy the entire event space, with only Brownstone operatives left in the space at this point.

His actions culminate in a one-on-one showdown with the leader of a group of Bosnian mercenaries contracted by Brownstone. Despite displaying ruthless tactics against his other opponents, Fitz makes the interesting decision to fight the villain honorably, rather than shooting him dead right away. Initially, his choice comes across as a mistake, as the mercenary gets the upper hand and seemingly has Fitz on the ropes. But unbeknownst to him, Fitz had attached two parts of an explosive device on his back and chest, allowing him to blow an explosive hole in the man's torso.

It was a finishing move that had somewhat of a sci-fi edge to it, but still felt consistent with the technologically advanced arsenal of weapons Fitz had at his disposal throughout the movie.

Fitz also had a small helping hand from the recently fired sheriff of the community, Olivia Thirlby's Parker. Having infiltrated the party as well, Parker was able to take on a minor role in the action, including a chance to kill Garret Dillahunt's character when he had Fitz in his sights. Although less skilled than his foreign counterparts, Dillahunt's character made it surprisingly far, but ultimately, none of the villains went unpunished - and that extended to the one power player who managed to keep his distance from the entire conflict.

In the closing minutes of the movie, Fitz travels to the Middle East, where he targets the company’s founder and leader. Fitz uses a sniper rifle to shoot him in the head, thus bringing Brownstone’s reign of terror to a complete end, tying up the last remaining loose end.

It was the methods of the aforementioned villain who made all of this necessary. Desire for full control over the region's water, which would lead to the construction of AI data centers and in turn, a vast increase in the company's wealth, was the driving force of his decision making.

As is the case with every AI data center, a significant amount of water is needed in order to keep them going. Brownstone recognizes this and, as such, is actively working to build cooling centers that would help keep the technology at a healthy temperature. For this, the company needs a sizable amount of land, and they had identified the town of Valentine in the countryside of Wyoming as a prime place for their cooling centers.

In its efforts to make sense of the lengths they were willing to go to get what they wanted, Ghost Soldier addressed the matter of imminent domain, a law that enables property to be seized if it serves the good of the community. As characters in the story pointed out, the villains would have had to wait longer than they preferred for imminent domain to kick in, and expectations placed on them to get results spurred them to take matters into their own hands.

Brownstone is no more, but Fitz still has more to do. His handler in the government, played by Shea Whigham, threatened to pull him out of Wyoming, prompting Fitz to tempt him with a compelling offer. Fitz has thus far been lying low in his lab at Wyoming, even when he knows the government could use him elsewhere. Taking advantage of this, Fitz promised to help deal with international threats if he was allowed to finish the Brownstone fight.

Presumably, that's what will define Fitz's next chapter. The United States has all sorts of problems to concern itself with, from Russia to China, which were both brought up in their conversation. It's likely that in the immediate aftermath of Ghost Soldier, Fitz will have his hands full with field work overseas. That setup could create room for a sequel if the new Jim Caviezel-led action film performs well at the box office.

A reclusive government asset and former Green Beret veteran uses his weapon prototypes to defend rural communities in Wyoming.

#3442. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care? In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3441. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3440. Prime Video's 2-Season Action Thriller Just Surged 307% To Become the No. 1 Streaming Original

When it comes to the host of action thrillers that you can find on Prime Video, none have made quite the waves that The Terminal List has. Based on the popular James Reece novels by former Navy SEAL-turned-author Jack Carr, the two-season drama has soared in the streaming charts, with Variety reporting that the show had even jumped into "No. 1 on Streaming" territory just last week. With over 1.3 billion minutes watched, the David DiGilio-created thriller continues to exceed expectations and is a reminder that the conspiracy-minded military thriller is as strong as ever.

For fans who have followed The Terminal List since the first season dropped back in 2022, this doesn't come as a surprise. Although initial reviews for the book-to-screen adaptation were not in the show's favor, the audience scores were exceptional. It wasn't long before Jack Carr famously noted that the show was made for fans, and the budding action franchise has been better for it. Rather than cater to whatever was safe or perhaps politically correct, the Chris Pratt drama largely stuck to its guns and pressed forward by expanding on what made the show successful in the first place, business as usual. That decision paid off, with the prequel, The Terminal List: Dark Wolf, and the second season, based on the novel True Believer, leaning more into the type of material fans were hoping for after that inaugural batch of episodes — even if there were some changes made to the source material. Over time, the show and its spin-off have become more well-received even by reviewers, and The Terminal List only continues to expand.

Of course, The Terminal List isn't just a successful show on streaming; it's one of Prime Video's best. Over the last several years, the Amazon platform has become known as the definitive home of the action thriller. Reacher and Jack Ryan alone would probably be enough to solidify this idea, but The Terminal List and its Dark Wolf prequel have proven over and again that there are differing flavors of the action/military thriller flavor that deserve our undivided attention. Sure, it can be a bit gruesome at times, but that's the world of espionage and off-the-books military operations for you. Pratt's James Reece is a protagonist haunted by his loss, one who seeks to redeem himself for the actions he took against those who wronged him — including his best friend. It's a harrowing but complex story that could only be told with the freedom that Prime Video offered DiGilio, Carr, Pratt, and the rest of the creative minds involved. The good news is, they're not done yet.

For those worried that the True Believer adaptation may be the end of the story, never fear. In Collider's interview with showrunner David DiGilio, the creator explained that they are always thinking of ways to expand The Terminal List world beyond just James Reece and Ben Edwards (Taylor Kitsch). While no official confirmation has been made as to what those projects may be (or their current status), we do know that the next James Reece story will be a book-to-screen take on the third Carr-penned novel, Savage Son, one that "Reecer" fans are anxious to see brought to life. How this will look exactly — as either a third season or a standalone series building off previous installments — is currently a mystery, but the news that the folks in charge have plans for a quicker turnaround is exciting. Hopefully, that means we'll also be getting more of the Dark Wolf prequel soon as well.

Although Chris Pratt may be best known for his big-screen roles in the MCU and Jurassic World franchises (or his time on the sitcom Parks and Recreation), The Terminal List has more than proven that the star has the chops to tackle more serious and thematic material with ease. "[He] was the person I thought of playing the role as I was writing the book," Carr once explained on his YouTube channel when speaking about the events leading up to the Prime Video series. And yes, that was before he was a well-known movie star. Sometimes things just work out, and in the case of The Terminal List, there's no doubt that Amazon made the right call in not only adapting these beloved military thrillers but also in finding its leading man. The next season can't come soon enough.

The Terminal List is available for streaming on Prime Video.

Woot has dropped the price of the JBL PartyBox 330 to $479.95 as an early Black Friday deal, saving you $150 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Beyond the discount, the PartyBox 330 has plenty to offer if you're looking for a speaker that can handle everything from backyard barbecues to larger gatherings—sitting between the smaller Club 120 and the larger PartyBox 520 in JBL's lineup, it delivers deep, punchy bass and enough volume to entertain a crowd, while its roughly 20-hour battery life means you can keep the music going all day without having to find an outlet. It's also rated IPX4 for water resistance, so a little rain or an accidental splash shouldn't be a problem.

That protection has limits, though—the 330 isn’t dustproof or particularly impact-resistant, so you’ll still want to be careful where you set it down. Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3438. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

Two and a Half Men is entering a new chapter in its history, which will give viewers a fresh way to watch the iconic sitcom.

Between 2003 and 2015, 12 seasons of Two and a Half Men aired on CBS as the series became one of the most successful sitcoms in modern television history. Despite all the drama that surrounded the show at its height, it seemed unlikely that it would continue to garner much attention once its finale aired. However, that has changed, as a new deal involving the Charlie Sheen sitcom has given long-time viewers a reason to talk about the series once again.

Variety has broken the news that all 12 seasons of Two and a Half Men will become available to stream on Pluto TV as of November 20. That marks the first time the sitcom will be available on an on-demand streaming service that is completely free for users to enjoy. Up until now, the show could only be streamed in America on Peacock with a paid subscription, since that was its exclusive home.

The move will bring the Sheen, Jon Cryer, and Ashton Kutcher show to its new home as part of a wider deal between Pluto TV and Warner Bros. TV. While the arrangement is surprising, it makes sense since both companies are now part of the holdings of Skydance Corporation. As Variety's report notes, Two and a Half Men is one of five Warner Bros. TV series that will soon become available on Pluto TV:

According to Variety's report, the currently announced series are part of what's being called the "first wave of programming" that will arrive on Pluto TV. That makes it fascinating to consider what other notable TV titles could make the leap in the future. For example, many of Chuck Lorre's other shows could become free to stream, given that most of his series are owned by Warner Bros. TV.

Thanks to the appeal of Two and a Half Men's characters and storylines, it was one of the most popular shows on television at the height of its success. Now, the avid viewers who helped make the sitcom a ratings behemoth will be able to enjoy the show for free in a matter of days on the Pluto TV website and through its app.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. Having recently passed what is likely its final box-office milestone, DC's new R-rated horror movie is on its way out of theaters. The movie will reportedly debut digitally after the first week of December, which gives it around three weeks to make the most of its remaining theatrical run. The film's release came at a particularly precarious period for DC Studios, and things have changed drastically in the weeks since its release. A few days ago, fans were met with the shocking news that co-CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran had been replaced after four years, leaving their planned slate in a state of flux.

In that regard, Clayface is lucky to have made it to theaters. The film began its journey as a spin-off to Matt Reeves' The Batman, with Mike Flanagan attached to write and direct, but was looped into the DC Universe and ultimately helmed by James Watkins. Reeves' universe continued with a sequel to The Batman and its spin-off television series The Penguin. There was also the third independent DC-related project in the form of Todd Phillips' Joker: Folie à Deux.

As recently as a few weeks ago, Gunn said that the long-term plan for the franchise doesn't rely on an interconnected universe. The series' previous iteration, the DC Extended Universe, was criticized for rushing toward a team-up film in the vein of Marvel's The Avengers. It remains to be seen if the franchise is rebooted once again after Gunn and Safran's departure.

Clayface remains mostly unconnected to the larger DC Universe, mainly because its version of Batman hadn't yet been introduced. The movie opened to mostly positive reviews from both critics and audiences. It's now sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 77% critics' score and a "Verified Hot" 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes — incredibly high for a body horror film. The aggregator website's consensus reads, "Carving out a unique identity for itself in the DCU while closely resembling a litany of body horror classics, Clayface takes time to get going until it eventually morphs into an icky and satisfying revenge thriller."

The movie, starring Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie, Max Minghella, and Eddie Marsan, debuted in more than 3,400 theaters three weeks ago. It'll enter its fourth week of release having lost more than 1,000 locations nationwide so far. Clayface has so far grossed $111 million worldwide against a reported budget of $40 million.

You can watch the movie in theaters ahead of its planned PVOD debut on December 8, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

Margot Robbie has been tapped to star in “The Week of Pain,” the next feature from writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, IndieWire has confirmed.

#3432. I hate how most smartwatches look, but I'll happily wear the Withings ScanWatch Light every day and with any outfit

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re after a beautiful smartwatch with all the basic fitness and health features you need, and which won’t ruin your outfit, look no further than the Withings ScanWatch Light 2. This elegant watch is pricey given its basic functionality, but still offers strong battery life and lots of insight via the companion app. If it’s bang for your buck you’re after, rivals offer more, but none can match the ScanWatch Light’s sheer pizzazz.

Auto activity detection didn’t work for me

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I hate most fitness trackers. Although I love what they do, I really don’t love how they look. For ages now, I’ve been pining for a smartwatch that does all the stuff I need it to when I’m at the gym or on a walk, yet looks like a normal, classic watch. I know, I know, you can set analog watch faces on many smartwatches, but we all know that’s not the same.

Enter the Withings ScanWatch Light. This thing is beautiful. It looks like a classic watch and fits in with even my smartest outfits. And it does all the basic fitness-y things I need it to, although not much more — the “Light” part really does mean light. This is not a feature-packed smartwatch, and certainly isn’t designed for athletes. Instead, it’s a smartwatch for people who want core health features without sacrificing style or ruining the cohesiveness of their outfits.

Find out whether this is the best fitness tracker for you in my full Withings ScanWatch Light review.

White/gray; rose gold/white; black/silver

The Withings ScanWatch Light costs $249 / £229 at Amazon. If you buy direct from Withings, you can choose a metal or leather strap for an extra $49, or a fabric strap for $39.

It certainly isn’t cheap, but look: Withings gear is always pricey. I don’t mind something being expensive if it can back up the price tag somehow. And most Withings products do so by combining charming design, solid build quality, and decent core functionality.

On the first two counts, the ScanWatch Light ticks the boxes. However, this is a stripped-back watch, so price versus functionality is pretty poor. You’re going to get more features for the money with the $249 Apple Watch SE 3. Or the $169 Amazfit Active Premium 3. Or heck, even the $79 Amazfit Bip 6. None match the ScanWatch Light’s elegant looks, though, so my question is: how much is style worth to you?

If you have the extra cash and want similar styling but more features, check out the ScanWatch Light’s bigger siblings: the $369 Withings ScanWatch 2 or $599 ScanWatch Nova.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In my opinion, the best thing about the ScanWatch Light is its design. I really appreciate the huge array of fitness features of smartwatches like my Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro. But I much prefer wearing a traditional analog watch when I’m not working out — giant AMOLED slabs and ugly silicone straps don’t really go well with my daily outfits. So, up to now I’ve switched between my analog watch and smartwatch when going to/from the gym, which has been a pain.

The ScanWatch Light is the perfect solution. It looks just like a classic analog watch: simple, elegant, beautiful. The face measures 1.4 inches, which fits my wrist nicely without feeling too bulky.

The watch comes in three different colorways (white/gray, rose gold/white, and black/silver). I chose the black model and love its effortless style and sophistication. It pairs well with all my outfits, from casual daily and smart casual fits up to suits and even my black tux. And the silver bezel and accents pair nicely with the silver and white gold rings I wear on my left hand. Obviously, though, the ScanWatch Light is also a fitness tracker! Which means I have a single watch for both gym, work, and leisure. I never have to switch again.

The standard strap is fluoroelastomer (a type of rubber), so it doesn’t absorb sweat or go gross when working out, and doesn’t chafe either. That said, while I usually dislike the look of rubber/silicone, the ScanWatch Light’s strap is finished with a matte effect, meaning it doesn’t look tacky like my (much cheaper) Amazfit Active. Again, you’re getting the best of both worlds.

I found the strap either a little snug or slightly too loose. In other words, I’m between sizes. This depends entirely on the individual anatomy/width of your wrist, though, so I’m not moaning. And besides, it still wasn’t uncomfortable at all, either when exercising or wearing all day — helped by the ScanWatch Light’s low 0.9-ounce kerb weight.

The buckle is dual-sided, meaning it also serves as a fixed loop to hold the strap tail in place, and there’s a sliding free loop for a second securement point. It’s a solid system and keeps the strap tail from flapping around. It can be a bit fiddly getting the strap through the second buckle opening, though.

As I’d expect from a Withings product, the ScanWatch Light is built extremely well and feels premium. The case is made from stainless steel and the face is covered by Gorilla Glass (the kind used on smartphone screens) so should stand up to daily wear and tear without scratching. It’s waterproof down to 5ATM (five atmospheres) of pressure, so you can take it swimming.

The digital grayscale OLED display is very small, but deliberately so — this is designed to be as minimalist a smartwatch as possible. When you press the digital crown, the watch hands move out of the way of the screen automatically if they need to, which I love. When it’s not in use, the display stays off and thereby blends in nicely with the black watchface, thus not spoiling the analog aesthetic. On the lighter models, though, the black display is always visible.

You control the watch entirely via the steel digital crown. Navigating the menu is fairly clunky, especially when you want to go back through menus. However, the menu system and features aren’t complex to begin with, so it’s fine. You don’t need to use the crown to set the time or date, as it’s all done digitally by pairing the watch to your phone and the Withings app.

As I mentioned up top, this watch bears the “Light” moniker for a reason. If you’re after highly detailed tracking and plenty of on-wrist control/info, the ScanWatch Light isn’t for you.

Don’t get me wrong, there’s a decent array of activities on offer. All the basics are there, of course: running, cycling, rowing, etc. There are indoor versions for treadmills and exercise bikes, as well as some specific activities like badminton, muay thai and more. There’s even a dog walking activity — I’m not sure how much that differs from ordinary walking.

None of the activity modes I used were particularly in-depth, though. Weight lifting, for example, had no interval functionality. They all seem to just measure BPM as you work out. Still, that’s all I really need. (And to be honest, I find the interval weight lifting function on my Amazfit watches a bit fiddly anyway.) You have no real control over the activities on-watch either — you simply use the digital crown to pause and then either resume or stop activities. Nor do you get any detailed info on the watch itself as to your performance or progress.

If you’re a serious fitness enthusiast and want something for hardcore training, you’ll want more in-depth measurements and onboard controls. Check out the Apple Watch Series 12, Withings ScanWatch 2 or Amazfit Active Premium 3. Or the Apple Watch Ultra 3 if budget is no constraint.

What the ScanWatch Light measured was pretty accurate. I compared the BPM analysis and calorific burn to several different machines at my gym and got essentially the same results each time, usually within just a couple of BPM and a couple of dozen calories. The ScanWatch did tell me I had mild bradycardia at first, measuring 52BPM resting. Look, I’m not in terrible shape, but that’s athlete levels, and I was highly stressed at the time due to a bereavement. So go figure. Since then, though, BPM reads have stayed more realistic and consistent. There’s also a VO2 max assessment available via the app — arguably the most important metric to track, generally speaking.

Unfortunately, the ScanWatch Light’s automatic activity detection simply doesn’t work on my test sample. Anything I did at the gym just went completely undetected. I cycled hard for 8 minutes. I ran for 10 minutes. Nothing, until I started the activities manually. I thought it might use GPS movement to detect activities, but when I walked or jogged outside, nothing happened. Weirder yet, on two occasions I've woken up in the night to find the watch has started detecting a run while on my bedside table.

I’ve reached out to Withings to find out why this may be and whether it’s an isolated incident on my test sample. This isn’t a gamechanger for me — I often find automatic detection results in false starts on my Amazfit Active and T-Rex 3 Pro, so I typically disable it anyway. But if a product has a feature, I still expect it to work.

The ScanWatch Light doesn’t have built-in GPS, instead relying on your phone for location services. This means you’ll need to keep your phone on you when you exercise if you want to view routes.

Health tracking-wise, it’s a similar story. The ScanWatch Light doesn’t track much. It’ll measure your BPM as I mentioned above, but there’s no ECG, blood oxygen, or body temperature tracking — you’ll have to upgrade to the pricier ScanWatch 2 or ScanWatch Nova for those.

Aside from BPM, the ScanWatch Light can track your sleep quality and give you an assessment of your breathing quality during sleep — both found on the pricier ScanWatch 2. There’s also menstrual cycle tracking. It’s more of an app feature, but you can add cycle tracking to the watch menu to input your stages. As a dude, I obviously didn’t use this, but it’s still a fundamental feature I expect to see in a fitness tracker.

There’s also a relaxation mode, which is pretty cool. You set a time interval, then how many breaths per minute you want to take. The watch then vibrates to prompt your breaths in and out. It’s a cool little feature for quickly taking a wellbeing break. And there are standing prompts when the watch detects you’ve not stood for a while — all pretty par for the course.

The Withings app is usually one of our favorites. It allows you to customize the ScanWatch Light’s menus and offers lots of information and data based on your measurements, inputs and watch readings. You can track your activities, progress and health data, with lots of graphs for visualization. The app provides a strong basic level of insight for all of this, explaining what terms mean and often linking out to informative articles for detailed explanation. As you can see in the screenshot below, I've tapped through from my BPM graph, to a basic explanation and second chart, and again through to a full detailed heart rate explainer article.

Via the Withings app, all your health data can be synced from centralized apps, like Apple Health, Google Health, or Samsung Health. Withings also partners with major tracking apps like Strava and MyFitnessPal, although if you’re using an iPhone like me, all this is routed through Apple Health to begin with anyway, so I didn’t need to set up any specific connections.

After one week with constant use and workouts 4-5 times per week, I still had 33% of battery left. So you can reasonably expect around 10 days with normal usage. A full charge takes around 2 hours on average, and charging via a 15W charger from 30% took me around an hour and 15 minutes, which tracks with Withings’ claims.

I’m not a fan of the ScanWatch Light’s charging dock. It’s just an awkwardly long piece of thin, bent plastic with an ostensibly meaningless lip on one side. It doesn’t sit particularly well on my bedside table, looks ugly, and struggles to stay in position. Great.

I much prefer the small, unobtrusive dock of my T-Rex 3 Pro, and Apple’s sleek little magnetic dock. But in fairness to Withings, I resent using all docks equally as much — they’re just a sad reality given that sticking a USB-C port on a watch would seriously compromise pressure- and waterproofing.

Look, the Withings ScanWatch Light is overpriced and under-featured for the money. I can admit that. It’s not for athletes or serious fitness enthusiasts. But it isn’t meant for those people. It’s for people like me who want a stylish all-round watch that can track all the basics for general day-to-day fitness and wellbeing without getting too serious. And importantly, for people who don’t want an ugly square hunk of AMOLED display on their wrist, clashing with their outfit.

It’s also built beautifully, has solid battery life and offers lots of visualizations and information via the Withings app. And did I mention it looks fantastic? I know the ScanWatch Light isn’t perfect, but damn, do I love it.

#3431. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3430. Final Fantasy 9: Melodies Of Life Officially Announced

Square Enix has officially announced a new Final Fantasy 9 release called Melodies of Life, and fans of what is arguably the best single-player entry in the series may want to make sure they can obtain it. The 2000 PS1 classic is one of the most beloved installments in the franchise, and it’s been years since fans have been asking for a remake of Final Fantasy 9, especially given how many rumors around it have emerged. The game’s 25th anniversary went by without the remake’s announcement, so hope is running dry, but fans are as passionate as ever.

They’ll also be delighted to know that the iconic JRPG isn’t being ignored entirely. Despite the lack of a remake announcement, Square Enix has officially announced a new FF9 release, Melodies of Life, according to a new report by Game Rant. Anyone who has played the RPG will recognize that title; Melodies of Life is the name of the main vocal theme in Final Fantasy 9, and the romantic theme for Zidane and Garnet’s relationship. This new release is a music box that plays precisely that song in all the heartwarming notes that only a music box can provide.

As seen in the report, the new product is called Final Fantasy IX Music Box - Melodies Of Life Wave 2, because this isn’t the first time this product has been sold. In fact, it has been released before, so this is a re-release, now available for purchase on the official online Square Enix Store in North America. The new Final Fantasy 9 release is being sold for $25.99. It’s a brown-colored music box with the silhouettes of Zidane and Garnet on the top. The Melodies of Life music box is part of a much wider collection.

In addition to the Final Fantasy 9: Roses of May music box, featuring Beatrix’s iconic theme song, there are music boxes for several other themes from games in the series, like Zanarkand from Final Fantasy X, the opening theme from Final Fantasy, and more. You can even find music boxes for other Square Enix franchises, like the Weight of the World music box from NieR: Automata. Of course, Melodies of Life is the most iconic song from Final Fantasy 9, and the re-release of the music box is a great opportunity to have it at home.

As a proud owner of said music box and a die-hard Final Fantasy 9 fan, I highly recommend the product. It’s not as good as a remake of the game, not that the classic has aged poorly, but it is a small reminder of how great the title is. For now, we fans will have to content ourselves with smaller releases. The rumors say that the project does exist, but that the Final Fantasy 9 remake has been halted, with no estimate as to when development will resume.

It may still take a while, as Square Enix’s main development segment seems focused on delivering the third and final part of the FF7 Remake series, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, and if the rumors are true, it will even have post-launch DLCs. As such, it may take a while before we even hear of a Final Fantasy 9 remake, if it exists, but the Melodies of Life music box is a more than welcome release while that doesn’t happen.

#3429. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas? Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3427. Matt Damon’s WWII Masterpiece Is Still His Greatest Movie 28 Years Later

There have been many high points in Matt Damon’s filmography, from soaring epics like The Odyssey to tense dramas such as The Departed, as well as action spectaculars like the Bourne franchise. One movie made relatively early in his career, however, stands out as one of his all-time classics. Saving Private Ryan, directed by Steven Spielberg, staked its claim as one of the most impactful war movies of all time when it was released in 1998 and, nearly three decades later, has lost none of its mastery.

Set in 1944, during the latter stages of World War II, the film brings us into the US War Department, which has received word that three of four Ryan brothers have been killed in action, with the fourth, James (Damon), missing in action. Due to a military policy of sending surviving siblings home in order to spare a family losing all their sons, Captain John H. Miller (Tom Hanks) is tasked with leading a detachment of soldiers to find Private Ryan. The eight men wade through the rubble of occupied France, risking their lives and facing personal demons on their way to finding their man.

It’s a fictional story based on the experiences of real-life veterans — in particular the Niland Brothers, three of whom were killed or captured while serving their country, meaning the surviving brother was sent home to complete his service. Spielberg went to great lengths to ensure accuracy in his film, including sending key cast members to boot camp to prepare them to play soldiers, although, notably, Damon was left out of the training in order to create separation between him and his co-stars.

Having covered one man’s quest to save as many as he could from the horrors of The Holocaust in Schindler’s List, Spielberg returned to the war movie genre to dramatize one of the bloodiest moments in the Second World War, the D-Day landings on Normandy’s Omaha Beach. The opening sequence, set during the landing, is approximately 24 minutes and is still unmatched in terms of portraying the violence and chaos of being on the front line. Through a variety of techniques, the Oscar-winning filmmaker puts you in the sand with the soldiers, making the experience a sensory overload and leaving you in no doubt as to what these men went through. The sequence was said to be so realistic that the United States Department of Veteran Affairs created a helpline for World War II veterans affected by seeing the film. It is brutal, harrowing, and sets the tone for the kind of story Spielberg wants to tell.

Although the mission in the story itself was fictional, the masterful work was symbolic of the many individual quests that soldiers undertook during the war, something Spielberg would later explore further alongside Hanks in their TV biopic Band of Brothers. As the poster’s tagline said, “The Mission is a Man,” and the film focuses on personal journeys, such as Miller’s Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, or his soldiers placing bets on what he did before the war. The stories, disagreements, and individual encounters along the way represent a vast patchwork of experiences that were had by millions of those fighting, many of which were lost to time. A heart-felt tribute to sacrifice, Spielberg’s final movie of the 1990s ensured he ended the decade with a flourish.

Still only in his late 20s, Damon had recently found success as a leading man in Good Will Hunting, which won him an Oscar for his and Ben Affleck’s script. As Private James Francis Ryan, he was not the star of the movie, but he was the center around which the plot was built. The group of soldiers go through Hell to find him, with all the horrors they endure leading them to believe this young man must be worth it. When they arrive at their goal, they discover an ordinary young man, just like them, keen to do his duty and not leave his comrades behind.

The climactic fight, as well as the emotional coda, also underline what we owe to those who gave their lives for our freedom. In the final moments of their time together, Captain Miller tells Private Ryan to “earn it.” In other words, live a life that was worthy of the sacrifices made for him. It’s a question that Spielberg’s film asks his audience – how does one “earn” the sacrifices made? For Ryan, it was living a good life, making the most of every day. At that moment, Damon’s character becomes the film’s lesson as well as its mission.

There are few films that have endured as long as Saving Private Ryan, thanks to its focus on the soldier’s experience, vivid battle scenes, and rousing patriotism. While Matt Damon would have bigger roles to come, being at the core of this classic is still one of his most impressive achievements.
