#3426. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3424. James Gunn's DCU Exit Deals A Huge Blow To Upcoming Superman Series

After a massive shake-up, it has been confirmed that both James Gunn and Peter Safran have exited from their leadership roles at DC Studios. Although Gunn and Safran had originally signed four-year contracts starting November 1, 2022, their departure is surprising because they were expected to have a longer run. With this massive new shift, it is hard not to wonder how the upcoming Superman series will be affected.

Although Skydance has not officially addressed the reason behind this shift, it can primarily be attributed to the underwhelming box office performances of movies like Clayface and Supergirl. Gunn, too, has taken to social media (via Instagram) to express his relief surrounding his exit. He even confirmed that he and Safran are not done with DC or its superheroes and the characters they have set up will live on.

As reports confirm, Man of Tomorrow has already entered post-production, suggesting that it will not be heavily impacted by this new change in leadership. However, the same cannot be said about the upcoming Superman spin-off series, The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd. The project had already raised quite a few eyebrows when it was first announced, and now its future seems even more tricky.

Created by Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault, The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd has already finished filming and is set to eye a 2027 release. However, this new change in DC's leadership seems to dampen its appeal in more ways than one. Although The People VS. Gorilla Grodd always seemed like a strange genre-bender, it was being treated as a vital connective tissue in the overarching franchise.

However, after Gunn's exit, it seems likely that his "Chapter 1: Gods and Monsters" blueprint will soon be discarded, with Skydance focusing more on fast-pacing projects with much wider appeal. While a new Justice League movie would still be exciting, more experimental additions like The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd would likely have no place in DC's on-screen future.

The comedic mockumentary interpretation of Grodd in the upcoming series was also expected to graduate to a mainline Flash or Justice League antagonist. Similar to Peacemaker and Creature Commandos, Gunn could have elevated Grodd into a formidable villain in the DCU's larger narrative. However, now, it is hard not to wonder if Grodd would fit into the Studios' long-term blockbuster plans.

Even the upcoming show's Daily Planet ensemble, including Skyler Gisondo (Jimmy Olsen), Wendell Pierce (Perry White), Beck Bennett (Steve Lombard), and Mikaela Hoover (Cat Grant), seems to be in a limbo after the new shift. Gunn's involvement almost promised a more cohesive and interconnected future for the crew.

While they will still retain their roles in Man of Tomorrow, their future beyond the franchise's 2027 run seems uncertain. This, in turn, makes The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd a lot less interesting.

While novel and distinct additions to the superhero genre are always welcomed, The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd always seemed like a strange and risky way of expanding the overarching franchise. Superhero fatigue still lingers, which is why the genre cannot stop reinventing itself to remain relevant and engaging. However, The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd felt like a wild swing for the franchise.

The show's satirical true-crime mockumentary approach risked cutting Grodd's credibility as a menacing villain even before he faced a superhero on the big screen. Experimental superhero spin-offs are also starting to become increasingly hard to consume because their ambition often outweighs their longevity. Take, for instance, shows like Wonder Man that earned critical acclaim but struggled to leave their mark.

Considering how the DCU has been far less experimental than the MCU, The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd is still exciting. It is hard not to be curious about what it will bring to the table with its offbeat idea. At the same time, though, the show demands careful optimism, given how the Superman spin-off series could be the last of its kind after James Gunn's departure.

Set in the same cinematic world as James Gunn's hit 2025 Superman feature film, this upcoming mockumentary miniseries centers around Gorilla Grodd's conviction for the murder of his father, a criminal case reopened by the Daily Planet's own Jimmy Olsen.

#3423. After ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back. My bet: he will not shoot another film in English and will stick to making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

Now he’s back to his self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “A Kukuku Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3421. The Cosmere Explained: Everything To Know About Brandon Sanderson’s Shared Fantasy Universe

Fantasy literature is more popular than ever, and the medium is always changing. Previously, it was considered "for nerds" and was a fairly niche community. In the 21st Century, however, things have opened up quite a bit, and fantasy literature has become much more mainstream and celebrated, and rightfully so, likely because it provides a method of escapism, free from the mundanity of everyday life.

While fantasy novels are a dime a dozen nowadays, some of them have made a larger mark on history than their peers. Among these historical feats is a massive undertaking that is still ongoing and will likely not conclude anytime soon. This ambitious, sprawling, and one-of-a-kind project is known as the Cosmere, which has been going strong with yearly releases for 20 years now. The name has been popular lately thanks to the creator scoring an adaptation deal with Apple TV. But what exactly is the Cosmere?

The Cosmere is a shared literary universe created by author Brandon Sanderson, beginning with his debut novel, Elantris, in 2005. The basic premise is that thousands of years ago, a god named Adonalsium was mysteriously shattered into 16 pieces called Shards. These Shards were scattered across the galaxy, each coming to rest within a particular solar system. Each stand-alone story or series takes place on its own planet within the same galaxy. Due to the influence of the Shards, many of these planets have developed unique magic systems, each of which is layered and complex. However, some stories also take place on worlds where no Shards are present. Moreover, while all Shards are known thanks to Sanderson's own words, what is not known is where they all are or what influence they have on their worlds — in fact, only a select few are currently accounted for. While there are still aspects of magic here, there are no complex systems available.

Not only is each planet different in regard to magic, but also in regard to geography. Some planets, like Sel from Elantris, are pretty similar to Earth. Others, however, like Taldain of the White Sand graphic novels, are completely different. Taldain is tidally locked, meaning it is permanently day on one side of the planet and permanently night on the other. There's also the barren, windswept world of Roshar, the burning world of Canticle, and the extremely alien planet Lumar, which doesn't technically defy physics but doesn't resemble any real planets that we know of.

The Cosmere isn't strictly relegated to one particular sub-genre of fantasy, either. Elantris is more of a Medieval fantasy, but others fit firmly into the categories of steampunk, romantasy, space fantasy, urban fantasy, and epic fantasy. The universe isn't relegated to one specific format either, as it consists of many short stories, novellas, novels, graphic novels, and even children's picture books. There are over 30 of these entries, with many more planned to come. Recently, the universe has even expanded to include tabletop role-playing games. Their status as canon is debated, but they do add a new level of interaction with the universe that fans love so much.

The primary way in which the broader Cosmere is connected is via a mysterious character named Hoid (that's one of his names, anyway). No matter which story you read, you're almost guaranteed to find him lurking somewhere. Sometimes, he plays a major role, aiding the protagonists on their quests, whilst other times he is nothing more than a brief glimpse in the background. No one yet knows who Hoid truly is or what he wants, but he seems capable of performing all types of magic, regardless of the system. Hoid describes himself as a Worldsinger, meaning he is a sort of magical bard who tells stories, plays a flute, and inspires others. He has also taken up other professions, though, such as carriage driver, pirate, and even a coat hanger (yes, really).

Hoid isn't the only Worldhopper, though he is the most prolific. Other Worldhoppers (that is to say, characters who can jump to other worlds) are present. There are also many shadowy organizations working behind the scenes, which seem to have a motive that spans the entire galaxy, though what these motives are have yet to make themselves clear. It's here that the Cosmere excels the most: keeping the reader invested (pardon the pun, for those who are already fans). Not only are there secrets to be revealed over the span of numerous series, but each world is meticulously designed and more singular and different than any other work of fantasy out there.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

One of the main reasons fans are constantly drawn to the Cosmere goes beyond its immersive worlds and varied settings. As any fan will tell you, there is some profound moral wisdom within the pages. Characters often give sage advice to others, which is also applicable to real life. Many of these tidbits are about perseverance, trauma, love, politics, and war. They show how Sanderson thinks and feels, and how he, like many of the greatest fantasy authors, believes there is good to be found, even amongst turmoil.

Another reason fans are drawn to the Cosmere is its diversity. The Stormlight Archive series, for example, mostly consists of People of Color, to the point that white people are rare. Other stories, like Mistborn, feature primarily white people, but still have their fair share of POCs. The stories also include numerous queer, neurodivergent, disabled, and gender non-conforming characters, and feature both women and men in leading roles. Within each race, various nationalities are represented as well, often bearing similarities to real-world cultures. This approach makes the story vastly accessible, to the point that no one feels alienated or left out. Everyone can see a little bit of themselves in at least one character.

Lastly, there's the "Sanderlanche," which occurs in pretty much every book. This term refers to a deluge of plot twists that happens all at once near the end, exposing Sanderson's outside-the-box thinking and pre-planning. None of these twists feel like deus ex machinae, either, and all make sense within their contexts.

The Cosmere has not ended, not by a mile. In fact, it has been said that we are only about halfway through everything, if not a little less than that, with more works planned for release over Sanderson's lifetime. Other authors, such as Sanderson's friend Dan Wells, are planning to collaborate on the project, too, meaning this prospect will likely end up turning into a five-decade affair, if not more. With each new series or stand-alone entry, the lore thickens, and new histories are introduced. Magic systems emerge, and the stories influence the whole Cosmere in unimaginable ways. Already, the Cosmere is one of the most comprehensive and expansive universes in all of fantasy, yet it still has a long way to go.

By the time it has concluded, the Cosmere might very well rival the legendarium of J. R. R. Tolkien, who penned an enormous mythology surrounding his beloved The Lord of the Rings trilogy. Tolkien's world is widely considered the most complex mythology ever written, with more and more of his work being revealed even today, decades after his death. While the histories of each planet in the Cosmere may not come close to Tolkien, the lore behind the universe as a whole might just. This lore isn't revealed through history books, but rather by natural revelation, as part of the narrative (supplemented by a few short appendices). It's enough that readers have even been able to piece together a distinct chronology, placing each story in an organized timeline. There is no doubt that this shared universe will eventually go down in literary history as a masterclass in writing — heck, it pretty much already has.

#3420. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3419. Disney Drops First Look At New Christmas Carol Adaptation With Perfect Scrooge For The Lead

Unlike the latest Johnny Depp vehicle adapting A Christmas Carol, many adaptations of one of Charles Dickens' most beloved classics are well-loved and garnered no shortage of critical acclaim. The Muppets certainly knocked it out of the park in 1992, and even before that, Disney had Mickey's Christmas Carol featuring Scrooge McDuck, predictably, as Ebenezer Scrooge. But for those seeking a more purely Scrooge McDuck-focused adventure in a similarly elegant, concise format, Disney and Marvel have the perfect holiday treat coming next week.

Uncle Scrooge: A Christmas Carol is coming out November 18, 2026, and is a 40-page comic book retelling the Dickens classic but more squarely focused on the Disney character's lore while still under the structure of Ebenezer Scrooge's Christmas Eve redemption story. Ahead of its Wednesday release, Marvel released a stunning preview showcasing the first five internal pages in which Scrooge shrugs off taking time to celebrate Christmas with his loved ones in favor of seeking out a golden asteroid. But soon enough, he's visited by the first of three ghosts set out to remind him of the real treasures he's taken for granted, as it dives into Scrooge McDuck's origins.

Opening with Scrooge breaking away from family as Donald Duck, Huey, Dewey, and Louie decide the golden asteroid can wait, Scrooge retreats to a familiar sight: his Money Bin. Diving into the coins to savor the feeling of his riches cascading around him, he's soon greeted by a familiar sight: a golden nugget from his early days panning for gold in the tributaries of the Yukon River. This brings out the Ghost of Christmas Past, triggering the visuals to change sharply to a painterly rendition of Scrooge's humble past as he encounters his first taste of riches. The preview ends with classic Scrooge McDuck antagonist Soapy Slick acting on a plot to rob him of his newfound riches.

Right away, the preview hits all the right beats for Duck Tales and general Disney fans to enjoy, from much of the Duck Family making an early appearance, to the gorgeous painterly visuals of the Ghost of Christmas Past's sequence. Seriously, the incredible artist team of Paolo Mottura, Fabio Celoni, Marco Mazzarello, and Francesco D'Ippolito alongside writer Louise Jones Simonson, colorist Arianna Consonni, and letter Joe Caramagna are enough of a selling point. But this glimpse is still a mere tip of the iceberg.

While fans were already treated to a fantastic glimpse of the Duck Family in the first pages, even the original solicits tease more characters to come, even more exciting given Soapy Slick was one such character not previously teased. Ludwig Von Drake and Gyro Gearloose are particular characters yet to appear, and Scrooge's past hasn't even concluded its portion yet, ending instead on a cliffhanger. But with this story seemingly more focused on retelling Scrooge McDuck's story in the framing of A Christmas Carol, rather than simply inserting him as Dickens' Scrooge character, means the story will evidently take a different, more fascinating direction and feeling more like an authentic reflection on his life up to this point.

One of Disney's earliest animated movies returns almost a century later this Christmas to celebrate a classic character's first adventure.

Thus, it feels more like a Scrooge McDuck story far removed from his Christmas on Bear Mountain debut, while still more focused in-depth on his foundations as a character than Donald Duck and the Christmas Carol, and especially more original than Mickey's Christmas Carol. It's unlikely to alter his personality to the core quite like the Dickens story, but it's also a thoroughly solid opportunity to dive into Scrooge's past, see what caused a shift toward obsession with wealth rather than quality time with family, while ultimately leading to a compromise. For Disney fans and those who want a fun dive into Duck Family lore, Uncle Scrooge: A Christmas Carol will be an essential read once it hits shelves on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

DuckTales (1987) follows the adventures of Scrooge McDuck and his grandnephews, Huey, Dewey, and Louie, as they traverse the globe in search of treasure and encounter various villains. The show combines elements of action and comedy, highlighting themes of family and bravery. A staple of Disney's animated television, DuckTales features a memorable cast and engaging storylines that have entertained viewers for decades.

#3418. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3416. Peacock Officially Replaces 'Suits' With a Legal Drama That Can't Be Beat

The USA network has tried for years to come up with a worthy successor to their hit legal drama, Suits. The nine-season series, which ran from 2011 to 2019, managed to capture the cutthroat, yet fascinating world of high-powered lawyers in New York City. Suits became even more popular years later when the show gained a whole new following after becoming available to stream on Netflix in 2023. Since Suits, USA has never managed to come up with a truly entertaining series that matches the show's smart writing and fun storylines — until now, that is.

In 1995, John Grisham published a popular novel called The Rainmaker. The exciting story, about a young attorney named Rudy Baylor (Milo Callaghan), was eventually adapted as a film in 1997, starring Matt Damon. The television version of the story kicked off its first season in October 2025. Rudy and his girlfriend, Sarah Plankmore (Madison Iseman), have just passed the bar and are both hired to work at a prestigious law firm in Charleston. But on Rudy's first day, he's fired by head lawyer, Leo Drummond (John Slattery), after speaking his mind. Rudy ends up working for the much less fancy firm, J. Lyman Stone, which is run by Jocelyn "Bruiser" Stone (Lana Parrilla, in a gender-swapped role that Mickey Rourke originated in the film). Rudy teams up with Bruiser and her right-hand man, Deck Shifflet (P.J. Byrne), as they take on an intriguing case involving a woman named Dot Black (Karen Bryson), who believes that the hospital where her son died is covering up something suspicious. The rest of the season unfolds with an action-packed story that fits perfectly into 10 fast-paced episodes.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

The Rainmaker, which just premiered its second season in October, manages to seamlessly blend several different genres. There are frightening, suspenseful twists in the storytelling one moment, and silly humor the next. No matter the tone of each scene, Rudy's story is that of a heroic underdog, and he serves as the perfect protagonist to highlight the many injustices in the legal system. He's also dealing with a painful past that continues to affect his life. The Rainmaker thrives with its unpredictable storytelling, but the series becomes a true standout because of its well-rounded characters. Even supporting characters end up providing valuable building blocks to the narrative. The relationships that form between the characters, especially the mentor connection between Bruiser and Rudy, or the buddy-cop feeling of Deck and Rudy's partnership, allow the series to offer both serious and lighthearted moments.

The Rainmaker could have fallen into second-rate television without its stellar cast. Callaghan offers a protagonist that is easy to root for, even when he's failing. It's also interesting to see the changes in Callaghan's delivery from Season 1 to 2, as he demonstrates the growth that Rudy has experienced. Parrilla is perfection as the tough-as-nails Bruiser, who is trying to forge her own path beyond that of her disgraced lawyer father. Slattery offers his sly, shark of a lawyer with aplomb, and Merle Dandridge takes over in Season 2 as his equally ruthless replacement. These lead actors help to create a solid framework for the series, but the supporting cast is every bit as impressive. Byrne provides much-needed comedic relief in the series as Deck, with a character that is constantly eating and making wise-cracks. Bryson also supplies the series with its quiet heart as the grieving Dot. Together, the entire cast elevates the series from a traditional legal drama.

If you were a fan of 'Suits', these shows will scratch that itch.

Although the show has only aired a few episodes of Season 2 so far, The Rainmaker has set up an even more captivating story revolving around a young boy who seeks out Rudy's help after he's unfairly sentenced to a juvenile detention center. Rudy and Deck realize there's something nefarious going on, and decide to investigate. Bruiser has her own case to worry about this season, when her ex-husband, Tom Cassady (Austin Nichols), requests she defend him. There are several more episodes to go before we reach the end of the season, but it's clear that The Rainmaker is not holding back in its second outing. If you haven't watched this entertaining series yet, we order you to binge-watch it today.

The Rainmaker is available to stream on Peacock in the U.S., with new episodes dropping every Friday on USA.

The Federal Aviation Administration began rolling out a massive new A.I.-powered air traffic system nationwide just days before Friday's shocking ground stop ... and the timing is raising some eyebrows.

On Tuesday, the agency announced it was expanding its $875 million A.I. system, called SMART, to all 22 air traffic control centers ... promising fewer delays, less fuel consumption and smoother travel.

But just three days later, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop ... throwing air travel into chaos.

As Gizmodo reported, the rollout had already sparked concerns ... with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association saying it wasn't involved in designing or testing the technology.

The FAA insists the A.I. only recommends flight routes, leaving final decisions to human controllers. Worth noting ... so far, there's no evidence linking SMART to the shutdown.

As TMZ previously reported ... the ground stop halted departures nationwide, sparking chaos at airports across the country as travelers were left stranded.

For now, the cause of the shutdown remains under investigation.

#3414. Netflix’s 8-Part Horror Series Deserves Kudos For Reimagining A 187-Year-Old Masterpiece

Some of the greatest horror shows are adaptations, but not every horror adaptation is great. In the past, many TV shows and movies have attempted to translate the works of iconic horror authors to the screen. While Stephen King remains one of the most adapted horror authors, even the works of H.P. Lovecraft, Shirley Jackson, and Edgar Allan Poe have been picked up for adaptations.

Speaking of Edgar Allan Poe, most on-screen adaptations of his work have been direct translations. However, there is one Netflix horror show, The Fall of the House of Usher, that completely reimagines his entire line of work. Created by Mike Flanagan, The Fall of the House of Usher borrows its title from one of Poe's most popular horror stories.

However, instead of being a perfect book-to-screen take on the horror author's short story, the Netflix horror miniseries brilliantly modernizes its narrative while grounding it in relatable modern-day concerns. While at it, the Mike Flanagan show on Netflix also presents itself as a love letter to Edgar Allan Poe's works, dropping a massive number of references and nods to his poems, stories, and real life.

Edgar Allan Poe's The Fall of the House of Usher unfolds in a 19th-century estate, following the decay and the rot that has dawned upon the titular family. The original story dabbles more with themes of the inescapable, hereditary rot of one's bloodline by solely focusing on twin siblings, Roderick and Madeline. The tragedy from their lineage rot affects no one but them.

Mike Flanagan's Netflix show only borrows the foundational elements of the original story. It then goes on to expand its vision by becoming a biting critique of modern capitalism and the cost of greed. Instead of solely focusing on Roderick Usher's gradual loss of sanity, the show walks through the deaths of the entire Usher family's lineage, with each death drawing from one of Poe's stories or poems.

In the Netflix series, Roderick Usher's obsession with leaving his mark on the world and earning endless wealth is exposed as hollow narcissism. He seems far more morally skewed than his literary counterpart. Even his unchecked corporate greed and desire to grow his pharma dynasty at any cost serves as an intriguing parallel to the real world's opiod crisis.

While giving Edgar Allan Poe's classic story a modern interpretation, the Mike Flanagan series features references to everything from The Masque of Red Death to The Black Cat. Like most of Mike Flanagan's creations, it also does not shy away from drawing from Stephen King's books.

Mike Flanagan's horror adaptations never disappoint. So far, he has delivered brilliant takes on the works of Stephen King, Shirley Jackson, Henry James, Edgar Allan Poe, and Christopher Pike. Considering his near-perfect record, he seems ready to adapt H.P. Lovecraft's stories for the screen. The ambiguous nature of Lovecraftian cosmic horror makes it incredibly challenging to adapt.

However, given how H.P. Lovecraft, too, was inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, Flanagan has already proven his ability to translate abstract, unsettling horror ideas to the audiovisual medium. Flanagan is also directing a remake of Stephen King's The Mist, which is touted as one of the most Lovecraftian stories written by the King of Horror.

Mike Flanagan already has his eyes set on massive horror adaptations like The Dark Tower. However, it is hard not to hope that he will also give H.P. Lovecraft's stories a chance, especially after Netflix's The Fall of the House of Usher.

Loosely based on the story by Edgar Allan Poe, The Fall of the House of Usher is a horror drama mini-series created by Mike Flanagan (Midnight Mass, The Haunting of Hill House) for Netflix. This modern retelling follows a corrupt pharmaceutical CEO, Roderick Usher, as he is forced to reckon with his past as a curse begins to claim the lives of each of his children.

#3411. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3410. FAA Nationwide Shutdown Not Connected to Microsoft Outage: Report

The nationwide Federal Aviation Administration shutdown is not connected to Microsoft's widespread outage ... despite the timing of the two major disruptions raising questions about whether a cyberattack or technical failure could be behind both incidents, according to reports.

NBC News correspondent Tom Winter reports he's been speaking with top law enforcement and cybersecurity officials throughout Friday, and as of 5 PM ET, there's no indication the Microsoft outage has any connection to the FAA problems.

Winter says officials have found no evidence linking the two incidents, pushing back on speculation that Microsoft's technical issues may have played a role in the aviation disruption. The FAA has not publicly confirmed or denied whether the two incidents are related.

The clarification comes amid a chaotic day for travelers, with the FAA's nationwide shutdown raising concerns about flight operations across the country.

As we previously reported, the FAA ordered the unprecedented ground stop Friday afternoon, instructing departing flights at airports nationwide to remain on the ground because of what officials described as an extraordinary circumstance.

Planes already in the air were allowed to land, while international arrivals were being handled on a case-by-case basis. The order sent airlines and airports scrambling as passengers faced delays and uncertainty about when normal operations would resume.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FAA technicians were investigating the communications failure. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other national security threat, describing the incident as a telecommunications outage.

Meanwhile, Microsoft has been dealing with its own massive outage, which began Thursday and affected millions of users worldwide. Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint and other Microsoft 365 services experienced disruptions, impacting businesses, government agencies and other organizations.

Microsoft has attributed its problems to a technical issue involving a network capacity upgrade and subsequent network changes, saying it found no evidence of malicious or cyber activity. The company had begun restoring services Friday, although some users continued experiencing issues.

Despite the overlap, Winter's reporting suggests the two major outages are separate incidents, with officials not finding evidence that Microsoft's technical problems contributed to the FAA's nationwide shutdown.

The FAA's investigation into the communications failure remains ongoing.

#3409. This 106-Minute James Bond Thriller Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Paramount+

The James Bond franchise was at a crossroads before the decision to hire Daniel Craig to play the iconic spy. While Pierce Brosnan’s tenure was prolific (especially compared to the glacial pace of the Craig films’ release schedule), the series had largely veered into the world of unfashionable (at the time) wacky camp by its 2002 finale, Die Another Day, and the character was in need of a refresh, like Batman after 1997’s Batman and Robin. And like 2005’s Batman Begins, Craig’s first outing, Casino Royale, was a tightly focused origin story that put the character in a grim pressure cooker that would teach him the tools of the trade. But unlike Batman Begins’ all-timer follow-up, Casino Royale’s sequel Quantum of Solace was a mixed bag at best, widely criticized for squandering the first film’s setup in favor of a generic spy thriller. Whether that reputation is deserved is up for debate, but its upcoming departure from Paramount+ on Novemner 19, 2026, should encourage a second look.

Casino Royale followed a fresh James Bond in a high-stakes poker game working to disrupt the machinations of the terrorism financier Le Chiffre (Mads Mikkelsen) while finding himself falling for the double agent Vesper Lynd (Eva Green). Vesper’s ties are complicated by her actions in the movie’s back half, and her possible allegiance to an organization pulling the strings through Le Chiffre: Quantum. Casino Royale is elegant and methodical, more patient and suspenseful than a Bond film had ever been, and was a richly rewarding debut for the actor. Quantum of Solace, meanwhile, immediately throws viewers into stunts and action setpieces filmed in motion sickness-inducing coverage, courtesy of director Marc Forster. The first 20 minutes alone have a car chase, a midair fight involving Bond being suspended from wires, and a hand-to-hand fistfight, making it clear that this is a meaner and more efficient Bond than usual.

There are many things that made Daniel Craig’s run as James Bond distinct. On one level, there’s the more serious storytelling that served as a corrective to the silliness and extravagant villains of past films; you won’t find a Moonraker in that five-film lineup. On the other level, there’s a sense of serialized storytelling that had become very popular by the 2000s, with each film theoretically leading into its sequel, setting up character dynamics, betrayals, and arcs from one film to the next. Where the previous Bond films had a somewhat casual attitude to plotting (you knew SPECTRE and Ernst Blofeld were the ultimate bad guys in the Sean Connery films, but they could take a couple movies off), the Craig films were indebted to their larger story to a fault. By 2015’s Spectre, this became a serious problem, with attempts to wrestle the previous three films into one solid continuity giving viewers headaches.

Due to some tangled rights issues, Eon Productions, the studio behind Bond, was not able to use SPECTRE in any films until then, which necessitated a different evil organization named Quantum. With Casino Royale’s somewhat unresolved ending suggesting that Bond had only taken down the first leg of the totem pole, it made sense for the sequel to follow up on that, digging into the organization’s sophisticated schemes to grab an unadorned plot of barren desert. With Vesper Lynd’s betrayal and death still haunting the spy, he’s forced into locations as disparate as Port-au-Prince, Austria, and Bolivia, seducing women like Strawberry Fields (Gemma Arterton) and killing men as needed to get to the bottom of Quantum’s goals. The movie’s as serious as Casino Royale but with a much more over-the-top story and far wackier setpieces.

While the best James Bond movies have a relatively relaxed pace that lets the agent immerse himself in a handsome, luxurious environment and operate in the world of subterfuge before the big stunt showcases, Quantum of Solace is off to the races so quickly that it’s hard to let yourself sink in. Besides the convoluted plot, its biggest failing is its roller-coaster pacing and lack of sense of pacing. But if you can get past the “James Bond Cliff Notes” nature of the story and the dizzying direction of the action scenes, it’s a worthy addition to the character’s filmography, in part because it’s so different from anything else the series had to offer — and maybe the closest the series got to the Cold War tone of 1963’s From Russia With Love, with a dash of Jason Bourne to ensure the series was following trends.

Eon Productions course-corrected with Quantum’s sequel, Skyfall, which was an operatic and personal story that joined Casino Royale to become one of the series’ highest regarded entries. Meanwhile, Quantum (the organization) would soon be retconned to being part of SPECTRE, with the movie’s mark on the series being erased as cleanly as possible. But seeing a lean James Bond film, where the globe-trotting and seductions are largely sidelined for fistfights and vehicle chases, is a novel experience, and more thrilling than ever, even if it's considered one of the actor's weaker entries.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.
